Or he concealed it so as not to be blamed for seeking a child at an advanced age and in old age [[The author's words "at an advanced age and in old age": in al-Sihah, *al-kibar* is old age in years, and the noun is *al-kibrah* with a fatha. Or his voice was faint because of his frailty and decrepitude, as in the description of an old man: his voice is faint, and his hearing is intermittent.

There is disagreement about Zakariyya's age (peace be upon him). It is said he was sixty, sixty-five, seventy, seventy-five, or eighty-five.

Recited as "wahana" with all three vowel patterns (wahana, wahuna, wahina). He mentioned the bone because it is the pillar of the body, the thing that holds it upright, and the root of its structure; when it weakens, the whole frame collapses and its strength falls away. Also, it is the hardest and firmest part of the body, so when it is weakened, what lies beyond it is weaker still. He used the singular "bone" (ʿaẓm) because the singular denotes the genus (jinsiyya, the notion of the kind as such). His intention was that this kind, which is the pillar and support and the strongest component of the body, has been struck by weakness. Had he used the plural, it would have indicated another meaning, namely that some of his bones had weakened but not all of them.

The assimilation of the sīn into the shīn (idghām) is reported from Abū ʿAmr.

He likened the whiteness of the hair to a flame of fire in its brightness, its luminosity, its spreading through the hair, its pervading it and taking hold of it in every direction, by the kindling of fire. He then presented this in the form of a metaphor (istiʿāra), and attributed the kindling to the place where the hair grows, which is the head.

He brought the whiteness in as a specifying accusative (tamyīz) and did not mention the head as a possessive noun, relying on the addressee's knowledge that it is the head of Zakariyya. For this reason the sentence is eloquent, and its eloquence is attested.

He sought a means to God through what had previously been granted to him of answered prayer.

It is reported of some of them that a man in need asked him and said: "I am the one you did a kindness for at such-and-such a time." He said: "Welcome to one who seeks a means to us through us," and fulfilled his need.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verses 5–6:

His mawali, who were his paternal kinsmen, his brothers and the sons of his paternal uncle, were the worst of the Children of Israel. So he feared for the religion (al-din) that they would alter it and change it, and that they would not conduct the succession (khilafa) over his community well. Therefore he asked for an heir from his own loins who would be righteous, one to be emulated in reviving the religion and following its precepts (marasim), ﴿who will inherit from me after my death﴾ (min warai ba'di mawti).

Ibn Kathir read "min waraya" with the vowel shortened (bi-l-qasr). This adverbial phrase (zarf) does not depend on khiftu (I feared), because that would corrupt the meaning, but on something omitted (mahdhuf). Or it is related to the sense of guardianship (wilaya) in "al-mawali": i.e., I feared the action of the mawali, namely their alteration and their poor succession, from after me. Or: I feared those who would take charge of the affair after me.

Uthman, Muhammad ibn Ali and Ali ibn al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with them) read: "khiftu al-mawali min warai" (I feared the mawali after me). This has two meanings. One is that warai means "behind me" and "after me," so the phrase is related to al-mawali: that is, they would be weak and unable to establish the affair of the religion, so he asked his Lord to strengthen them and support them with a guardian He would grant. The second is that warai means "in front of me," so it is related to khiftu, and the meaning is that they passed away before him and went on, and there remained none among them on whom one could rely or whom one could lean upon.

﴿from Yourself﴾ (min ladunka) emphasizes that he is a pleasing guardian, by its being attributed to Allah the Exalted and issuing from Him. Otherwise, "grant me a guardian who will inherit me" would suffice. Or he meant an innovation from You without a cause, because he and his wife were not fit for childbearing.

﴿who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾ (yarithuni wa yarithu). The jazm (apocope) is the answer to the supplication, and the raf' (nominative) is a description (sifa). Similar is ridan yusaddiqni (Qur'an 28:34).

From Ibn Abbas and al-Jahdari: "yarithuni warith al-Ya'qub" (who will inherit me, an heir of the family of Ya'qub), in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). From al-Jahdari also: "aw yarith" (or an heir), as a diminutive of warith, and he said: a small boy (ghulaym saghir).

From Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and a group: "warithun min al-Ya'qub" (an heir from the family of Ya'qub), meaning: an heir will inherit me through him, and this is called tajrid in the science of rhetoric (ilm al-bayan).

The inheritance intended is the inheritance of Shari'a and knowledge, because prophets do not bequeath wealth. It is said: "yarithuni al-hibra" (he would inherit me as scholar), and he was a scholar (hibr), and "yarith min al-Ya'qub al-mulk" (and inherit from the family of Ya'qub kingship). It is said: "warithtuhu wa warithtu minhu" are two dialects (lughatan). It is also said that "min" is partitive (lil-tab'id), not for transference, because not all the family of Ya'qub were prophets or scholars, and Zakariyya, peace be upon him, was of the lineage of Ya'qub ibn Ishaq. It is said: this Ya'qub is the brother of Zakariyya, Ya'qub ibn Matan. It is also said: this Ya'qub and Imran, the father of Maryam, were brothers from the lineage of Sulayman ibn Dawud.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 7:

"Samiyyan" (﴿a namesake﴾): no one had been named Yahya before him. This is evidence that beautiful names are worthy of being preferred, and the Arabs used to aim for them in naming, because they are more distinguished, more renowned, and further removed from being mocked (nabz). So much so that a poet, praising a people, said:

Beautiful of names, wearing waist-wraps (azr) trailing,
Red ones, brushing the ground with their fringes (hudb).

[It is said: "sana'a al-rajul" in the pattern of "zarufa," so he is "sani'" meaning handsome, and "asna'," and the woman is "sana'a," and "sana'" is the plural of "asna'," meaning their names are good, so they are more distinguished, more renowned, and further removed from being mocked. "Al-humr" is an adjective of "al-azr," and "tamassu" is another adjective of it. "Hudb" of a thing is its edge, and what suits the meaning is that the intended sense is the plural; it may be that it includes the singular, like "qufl," and the plural, like "fulk." It is also permissible that it is a collective noun, and for this reason its singular is "hudbah." Brushing the ground with the edges is a metaphor for their length, or rather for their wealth and prosperity, which necessarily entails that.]

Ru'ba said to the genealogist al-Bakri, when he asked him about his lineage: "I am the son of al-'Ajjaj." He said: "You have shortened it and made it known."

It was also said, on the authority of Mujahid, that "samiyyan" means "equal" or "like," as in His saying: ﴿Do you know anyone who is His equal (samiyyan)?﴾ The word "samiyy" is used for an equal only because each of two similar things is called by the name of its equal, its likeness, its form, and its counterpart, so each of them is a "samiyy" to the other. Similar to "Yahya" among their names are "Ya'mur" and "Ya'ish," if the naming is Arabic. They also named someone "Yamut," and he was Yamut ibn al-Mazra'. They said: there was no one like him in that he never disobeyed and never intended disobedience at all, and that he was born between an aged, decrepit old man and a barren old woman, and that he was "hasur" (chaste, one who does not approach women).

The meaning: "I am in the state of being barren, when I am young and old, so I was not given a child because one of the two causes was lacking. So when both causes are lacking, shall I be given one?" Then, if you say: why did he ask when he and his wife were in the state of decrepitude and barrenness? [[Mahmud said: "If you say, why did he ask when he and his wife were in the state of decrepitude... etc." Ahmad said: There is a problem with what he answered, because he committed himself to the view that Zakariyya found it unlikely that what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had promised would happen, and it is not permissible for a Prophet to utter what is not fitting, for the sake of a benefit that Zamakhshari specified and which could be achieved without it. The apparent answer, and Allah knows best, is that Zakariyya's request was only for a child in general, and the answer was given accordingly. The reply does not indicate that a child would be born to him while he was in old age, nor that it would be from his barren wife. So it was possible in his mind that the one promised would be born in this condition, and it was possible that their strength and youth would be restored to them, as Allah did for others.

Or the child might be from someone other than his barren wife, so he found it unlikely that a child would be born to them while they remained in their state, and so he asked whether it would happen while they were like that. It was said: "Thus," meaning: the child will be born while you are like that. The promise then referred to the very thing promised, and the difficulty was removed, and Allah knows best.]], when he was granted his request, did they find it unlikely and wonder at it? I say: it was so that he would be answered in the way he was answered, so that the believers would increase in certainty and the wrongdoers would be deterred. Otherwise, Zakariyya's belief, at the beginning and at the end, followed one path: that Allah is independent of causes. "Attaa" (عتيا) means: dryness and stiffness in the joints and bones, like a dry, withered stick. [[His statement "like a dry, withered stick" means dry, as stated in al-Sihah. (ʿAyn)]]

It is said: "ʿatā al-ʿūd" and "ʿasā" (عسا) from old age and advanced years. Or: they had reached, of the stages and degrees of old age, what is called "attaa." Ibn Wathhab, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the ʿayn with a kasra (عتيا), and likewise ṣaliyyā (صليا). Ibn Mas'ud read both with a fatha in them. [[His statement "with a fatha in them" perhaps means with a fatha on the letter. (ʿAyn)]] Ubayy and Mujahid read ʿasiyyā (عسيا). [[His statement "ʿasiyyā": in al-Sihah, ʿasā al-shaykh yaʿsū ʿasiyyā: he became old and aged, like ʿatā. (ʿAyn)]]

Kadhalika (the kāf is in the nominative case), meaning: the matter is so, a confirmation of what he said. Then he began: Qāla rabbuka (“Your Lord said”), or it is in the accusative governed by qāla. That (dhālika) refers to something vague which is explained by: "It is easy for Me" (huwa ʿalayya hayyinun) and similar, and "We decreed to him that matter: that the last remnant of these people would be cut off in the morning" (wa-qaḍaynā ilayhi dhālika al-amra anna dābira hāʾulāʾi maqṭūʿun muṣbiḥīn).

Al-Ḥasan read: wa-huwa ʿalayya hayyin, and this reading cannot be accepted except according to the first interpretation:

That is, the matter is as you have said, and He, upon that, makes it easy for Me. There is another interpretation: that dhālika refers to what preceded of Allah's promise, not to the statement of Zakariyya. Qāla (“He said”) is omitted in both readings: that is, He said, "It is easy for Me," and He said, "And it is easy for Me." If you wish, you need not supply it, since Allah is the one addressed; the meaning is that He said that, and His promise and His word are true.

"Shay'an" (a thing), because the nonexistent is not a thing; or "a thing that is counted." [[Maḥmūd said: "That was said only because the nonexistent is not a thing, or a thing that is counted…" Aḥmad said: He first restricted it to the plain literal sense of negation, which is the truth, because the nonexistent is certainly not a thing, contrary to the Muʿtazilah who say that the nonexistent that is possible is a thing.

From this, al-Zamakhsharī struggled to move from the first interpretation to the second by a kind of interpretation that suits the Muʿtazilī doctrine. So he made the negation apply to being a thing that is counted, although absolute thingness is established for the nonexistent in his view; the truth is that the apparent meaning remains in its place.]] Like their saying, "I marvelled at someone who is nothing," and his verse:

"When he sees something that is not a thing, he thinks it a man."
[[And the earth became narrow upon them until their fleer was... When he sees something that is not a thing, he thinks it a man.

He says: the earth became narrow for our enemies, because every path they seek, they think one of us is in it, so they turn back. The sensory narrowness is metaphorically borrowed for that, by way of explicit metaphor, until the one fleeing from them, when he sees something that is not a thing, thinks it a man of ours, and so turns back in fear. "Thing" is what exists, and what is other than it is the nonexistent; but it is borrowed for a small, worthless thing, since each one is not counted, by way of explicit metaphor, so that seeing it may properly be the object of sight.]]

And al-Aʿmash, al-Kisāʾī and Ibn Wathhāb read: khalaqnāka ("We created you").

That is: "Appoint for me a sign by which I may know the fulfilment of what You have given me good news of."

He said: "Your sign is that you will be prevented from speech, so that you cannot speak, while you are sound in your limbs and well-formed in body. There is no muteness or dumbness in you."

The mention of nights here, and of days in Aal 'Imran, indicates that his inability to speak lasted for three days and their nights.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 11:

"Awha" (he signalled): it is related from Mujahid that it means he gestured, and the verse "except by gesture (ramz)" (﴿إِلَّا رَمْزًا﴾) bears witness to this. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he wrote for them on the ground, "Glorify (Allah)" (﴿سَبِّحُوا﴾), "pray" (صلوا), or on the surface. And "an" (أن) here is the explanatory "an" (al-mufassira).

Meaning: take the Torah with determination (ḥadd), seeking support through success and reinforcement; al-ḥukm is al-ḥikma (wisdom). Among its uses is the line:

[[wa-ḥkum ka-ḥukm fatāt al-ḥayy (And judge as the young woman of the tribe judged) idh naẓarat ... ilā ḥamām sarrāʿ wārid al-thamad (when she looked at a swift pigeon coming down to the little water)

qālat alā laytamā hādhā al-ḥamām lanā ... ilā ḥamāmatinā wa-niṣfuhu faqad (she said: "Would that this pigeon were ours, and to our pigeon, and half of it, then that is enough")

fa-ḥabasūhu fa-alfawhu kamā wujidat ... sittan wa-sittīna lam tanquṣ wa-lam tazid (So they trapped it, and they found it as she had counted: sixty-six, neither less nor more)

It is by al-Nābigha, whose name was Ziyād, addressing al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir. The young woman is Zarqāʾ al-Yamāma, whose sharpness of sight became proverbial. She looked at a pigeon hastening to the water and said: "Would that the pigeon were two pigeons (ḥamāmatayn), and half of it were..., then the pigeon would be a hundred (mīa)." It fell into a hunter's net, and they found it was sixty-six pigeons, and half of it thirty-three; when all of them were added to her pigeon, they became a hundred. Al-ḥamām is every bird with a collar. Sarrāʿ is the plural of sarīʿ, described thus because it is plural in meaning, and wārid because it is singular in form. It is also transmitted as sharrāʿ with the shin marked, plural of shāriʿ. Al-thamad is little water.

The reading al-ḥamām wa-niṣfuhu with nominative case is on the basis that laytamā is non-operative (ihmāl). With accusative it is on the basis that it operates (iʿmāl), because mā is superfluous (zāʾida) and not restrictive (kāffa); otherwise ihmāl would be obligatory. It is also transmitted as aw niṣfuhu, where aw means wa (and), and the sentence contains an elided noun (muḍāf), since she wished that this pigeon and half of it would be hers. Ilā ḥamāmatinā is attached to an elided verb, meaning: joined to it. Qad is a noun meaning "enough (ḥasb)," annexed to the first person pronoun ya without the nūn of protection (nūn al-wiqāya), as one says ḥasbī. It is possible that the ya is a vowel-extending letter (ḥarf iṭlāq), so there is no annexation; but it is definite in the speech of Zarqāʾ, and the hāʾ in it is for pausing (sakt). This favours annexation in the speech of al-Nābigha. The fāʾ in fa-qad is superfluous, to embellish the utterance, like the fāʾ in fa-qaṭ; both mean "stop" (intahi). It may be the fāʾ of response, meaning: when you reach this limit, stop, as al-Saʿd (al-Taftāzānī) indicated in his Muṭawwal. Ḥabasūhu should be pronounced with shadda so that the verse is free of khabl, a kind of zaḥāf (prosodic licence) whose occurrence here is disliked.

It is also transmitted as ḥasabūhu, with the sīn before the bāʾ.]] It is said: ḥakama, yaḥkumu, ḥukman, like ḥalima, meaning understanding of the Torah and jurisprudence in religion, from Ibn ʿAbbās. It is also said: the children invited him to play while he was a boy, and he said: "We were not created for play," from al-Ḍaḥḥāk. From Maʿmar: intellect. It is also said: prophethood, because God had made his intellect firm in his childhood and revealed to him.

Hanānan (mercy) toward his parents and others, tenderness and compassion. Sibawayh recited:

"And she said, 'Hanān, what brought you here? Are you of a lineage, or are you one who knows this tribe?'
And the most recent sight I had of Umayna was a glance, as I stood on the side of al-'Ulyā."

"Then she said, 'Hanān, what brought you here? Are you of a lineage, or are you one who knows this tribe?'"

It is by Mundhir ibn Darham al-Kalbi, who says: "Aqrab 'ahd" means the most recent meeting or sight of Umayna, my beloved, the diminutive of Āmina. It is a glance I had of her beside that spot while I was standing there, that is, at the time of my standing there. In this is an indication that he was standing there, awaiting the sight of her. When she saw him, she said to him, "Hanān," meaning "my affair is Hanān," that is, mercy toward you. This is one of the places where the subject (mubtada') must be omitted because the predicate (khabar) takes the place of the verb, since it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) changed from the accusative. Her saying "mā atā bika hāhunā" is an exclamatory interrogative. "Adhu nasabin": that is, "Are you of a lineage, or are you one who knows this tribe?" It is also permissible that "adhu nasabin" is an apposition (badal) of the interrogative "mā" (what), meaning: "What compelled you to come here, or what led you to it, is a relative from the tribe, that is, your knowledge of it?" It is also permissible that the interrogation is genuine, and that she related it through the speech of another, so that he would be taught the answer by her saying "adhu nasabin..." etc., while she knew the reason for his coming, which was her love, so that someone from her family might ask him and he would answer with one of these two replies.

It was said: "Ḥanānan" means from Allah toward him. "Ḥanna" in meaning is to be at ease and to yearn, then it was used for tenderness and kindness. It was said that "ḥanān" is said of Allah just as "raḥīm" is said, by way of metaphor. "Zakāh" means purity; it was also said to mean charity, that is:

"He shows tenderness to people and gives charity to them."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 16–17:

﴿إِذِ﴾

Badal (substitution) from "Maryam" (Maryam).

Badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion), because the times include what is in them. And in it is that the purpose of mentioning Maryam is mentioning this time of hers, because this marvelous story occurred in it. Al-intibadh (withdrawal, the term for the act of "withdrawing" from others) means al-i'tizal (seclusion) and al-infirad (isolation): she secluded herself for worship in a place to the east of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), or from her household, withdrawing from people. It was said:

She sat in a raised place for ghusl (ritual bathing) from menstruation, screened by a wall or by something that covers her, and her place was the mosque. When she menstruated, she would move to her aunt's house, and when she became pure, she would return to the mosque. While she was in her place of bathing, the angel came to her in the form of a human young man, beardless, of bright face, curly-haired, well-proportioned in form, lacking nothing of the human form. Or [it means] he had a beautiful form and a balanced constitution. He appeared to her in human form only so that she would be at ease with his speech and not repelled by him; had he appeared to her in his angelic form, she would have been repelled and would not have been able to listen to his words. Her chastity and piety are shown by the fact that she sought refuge with God from that beautiful form, surpassing in beauty, and his representation in that quality was a trial for her and a testing of her chastity. It was said: she was in the house of her sister's husband, Zakariyya, and she had a separate sanctuary (mihrab) that she occupied; whenever Zakariyya went out, he would lock the door on her. She wished to find solitude in the mountain so that she could delouse her head, so the roof split open for her, and she went out and sat in the raised place behind the mountain, and the angel came to her.

It was also said: he stood before her in the form of a young man called Yusuf, a servant from among the servants of Bayt al-Maqdis. It was also said: the Christians took the east as a qibla because Maryam's place of withdrawal was to the east.

﴿الروح﴾: Jibril (Gabriel), because religion lives by him and by his revelation. Or God named him "His spirit" metaphorically, out of love for him and closeness to him, just as you say to your beloved: "You are my spirit."

Abu Haywa recited "rühana" (ruhana, "Our spirit") with a fatha, because he is a cause of what contains the spirit of the servants, and attaining "rawh" (rest/comfort) with God, which is the provision of those brought near, in His saying: ﴿فَأَمَّا إِنْ كانَ مِنَ الْمُقَرَّبِينَ فَرَوْحٌ وَرَيْحانٌ﴾ ("But if he is among those brought near, then there is rest and sweet provision"). Or because he is among those brought near, and they are the ones promised the "rawh"; that is, "our one brought near" and "one of our spirit."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 21:

The touching (al-mass) is made a metaphor for lawful marriage (al-nikah al-halal), because it is a euphemism for it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿before you touch them or have intercourse with women﴾. Fornication (al-zina) is not like this; rather, it is said of it: "he committed fornication with her" (fajara biha), "he defiled himself with her" (khabutha biha), and what is similar to that. It is not fitting that euphemisms and courtesies be observed in it.

Al-baghiyy: the unchaste woman who solicits men. According to al-Mubarrad, it is on the pattern fa'ul, originally "baghuwy," and the waw was assimilated into the ya'. Ibn Jinni said in his book Kitab al-Tamam: it is fa'il. Had it been fa'ul, it would have been said "baghuww," just as it is said: "fulan nahuww 'an al-munkar" (so-and-so is one who forbids evil strongly).

﴿And that We may make him a sign﴾: the reason clause, whose reasoned element is omitted. The meaning is: "And We did that so that he may be a sign for the people." Or it is coordinated with a hidden reason clause, meaning: "so that We may show by it Our power, and that We may make him a sign." A similar example is His saying: ﴿And God created the heavens and the earth in truth, and so that every soul may be recompensed for what it has earned﴾, and His saying: ﴿Thus did We establish Joseph in the land, and that We might teach him...﴾.

Maqdiyyan: decreed, determined, inscribed in the Preserved Tablet; there is no escape for you from its taking effect upon you. Or it was a matter fit to occur and to be decreed, because it is a sign and a mercy.

By "sign" is meant the lesson and the proof of God's power; by "mercy" are meant the laws and the gracious favours, and whatever is a cause for strengthening belief, reaching obedience, and righteous action. So it is worthy of being brought into existence.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 22:

On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: "She was reassured by his words, so he approached her and breathed into the opening of her shift, and the breath reached her belly, and she conceived." It was also said: the period of pregnancy was six months. And on the authority of ʿAṭāʾ, Abu al-ʿAliyah and al-Ḍaḥḥak: seven months. It was said: eight, and no child born at eight months survived except ʿIsa. It was said: three hours. It was said:

She conceived him in an hour, was shaped in an hour, and gave birth to him in an hour, when the sun had passed its zenith on that day. And on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: the period of pregnancy was one hour, just as she bore him, she cast him off. It was said: she conceived him when she was thirteen years old. It was said: ten, and she had menstruated twice before she conceived. And they said: every newborn cries out at birth [[His saying "ma min mawlud illa yastahillu ghayruhu" — in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "istahalla al-sabiyy" means he cried out at the time of birth. (ʿ)]]. So she withdrew with him (fa-intabadhat bihi), meaning she secluded herself while he was in her womb, as in the saying of the poet:

"They trample us with the skulls and the dust."

That is, they trample the skulls while we are upon them. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: "a tree that springs forth with oil" (tanbutu bi-l-duhni), meaning it grows with its oil in it; the prepositional phrase here is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥal). Qaṣiyyan: far away from her people, behind the mountain. It was also said: at the farthest part of the house. It was also said: she had been named after a paternal cousin of hers called Yusuf, and when it was said that she had conceived from fornication, he feared for her the king's killing, so he fled with her. When they were on part of the road, his soul prompted him to kill her, but Jibril came to him and said: "He is from the Holy Spirit, so do not kill her," and he left her.

﴿فَأَجاءَهَا﴾ (so the labour pains drove her): *ajā'a* is derived from *jā'a*, but after being made transitive its usage changed to the meaning of "compelling" (*ilja'*). Do you not see that you say: "I came to the place (*ji'tu al-makān*)," and "Zayd brought me to it (*ajā'anīhi Zayd*)," just as you say: "I reached it (*balaghtuhu*)," and "he made me reach it (*ablaghanīhi*)." Its counterpart is *ātā*, which is used only in the sense of "giving," and you do not say, "I came to the place (*ataytu al-makān*)," and "so-and-so brought it to me (*ātānīhi fulān*)."

Ibn Kathīr, in one transmission, read *al-makhāḍ* with a kasra. It is said: "The pregnant woman's labour pains began (*makhadat al-ḥāmil makhāḍan wa makhāḍan*)," and it is the movement of the child in her womb (*tamakhkhaḍ al-walad fī baṭnihā*). [[The words "and it is the movement of the child in her womb": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "the milk churned and was churned (*tamakhkhaḍa al-laban wa-stamkhaḍa*)," meaning it moved in the churn, and likewise the child when it moves in the womb of the pregnant woman. (Ā.)]]

She sought the trunk (*al-jidh'*) so that she might shelter herself behind it and lean on it at the time of birth. It was the trunk of a dry palm tree in the desert, having no top, no fruit, and no greenness. The time was winter. The definiteness (*al-ta'rīf*) here is of two possibilities. Either it is the definiteness of well-known names, like the definiteness of "the star" (*al-najm*) and "the thunderbolt" (*al-ṣa'q*), as if that desert had a palm trunk well known among the people, so that when one says "the trunk of the palm" it is understood from it to the exclusion of other palm trunks. Or it is the definiteness of the genus, meaning: the trunk of this particular tree, as if God, exalted is He, directed her specifically to the palm tree so that she might feed on its *ruṭab* (fresh dates), which is the suitable nourishment for a woman after childbirth, and because the palm is the most patient of trees in enduring cold, and its fruit comes only from its heart (*jumār*). Because of its suitability for her, together with the gathering of the signs in it, He chose it for her and compelled her toward it.

﴿مِتُّ﴾ (I wish I had died) is read with a *ḍamma* and with a *kasra*. It is said: "he dies (*māta yamūtu*)" and "he dies (*māta yamātu*)."

*Al-nasy'*: that which by right should be discarded and forgotten, like a menstrual rag and the like. Like *al-dhibḥ* (the slaughtered thing), the name of what is meant to be slaughtered, in the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَفَدَيْناهُ بِذِبْحٍ عَظِيمٍ﴾ (and We ransomed him with a great sacrifice). From Yūnus: when the Arabs departed from a dwelling, they would say, "Look after your *anṣā'* (leftover belongings)," meaning the small things such as a staff, a cup, and a *shiẓāẓ* (a stick inserted into the handle of a saddlebag). [[The words "and a shiẓāẓ": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "al-shiẓāẓ" is the stick that is inserted into the loop of the *jawāliq* (a sack). It also says "al-jawāliq" is a container. (Ā.)]]

She wished she had been a trifling thing, of no account, which by its nature and right is ordinarily forgotten, discarded, and thus finds the forgetting that is its due. This was because of the extreme shame and the fear of people's disapproval that overtook her, according to the human custom, not from aversion to God's decree, nor because of the severity of the obligation upon her, if they accused her (*idhā bahatūhā*) while she knew of her innocence and of the opposite of what she was accused of, namely that God had singled her out with the utmost majesty and honour. This was a slippery position, on which feet rarely hold firm: that you know your own joy at a great matter and a dazzling grace by which you deserve praise and merit exaltation, and then you see it, through the people's ignorance of it, as a fault for which you are reproached and blamed, or because of her fear that people might disobey God on her account. [[The words "if they accused her while she knew...": they attributed to her what was not in her. And *qarafat* means "she was accused." (Ā.)]]

Ibn Wathhāb, al-A'mash, Ḥamza, and Ḥafṣ read ﴿نَسْياً﴾ with a *fatḥa*. Al-Farrā' said: "Both are dialects, like *al-watr* and *al-watr*, and *al-jisr* and *al-jisr*." It is also permissible that it is a verbal noun used as a name, like *al-ḥaml* (the burden). Muḥammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazī read *nisa'* with a hamza, and it is diluted milk, which the people of the household mix with water because of its scarcity and meagreness. Al-A'mash read *mansiyyan* with a kasra, by way of *ittibā'* (vowel harmonization with the preceding letter), like *al-mughīra* and *al-mikhnar*.

From "min tahtiha" it is Jibril, peace be upon him. It was said: he would receive the child like a midwife (al-qabila). It was also said: it is Isa, and this is the reading of Asim and Abu Amr. It was said that "tahtiha" means below her place, as in His words ﴿تَجْرِي مِنْ تَحْتِهَا الْأَنْهارُ﴾ (﴿Rivers flow beneath them﴾). It was said: he was below her, beneath the sand dune, and he called out to her, ﴿أَلَّا تَحْزَنِي﴾ (﴿Do not grieve﴾). Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisai and Hafs read ﴿مِنْ تَحْتِها﴾ (with a kasra on the mim and the ha'), and the pronoun in ﴿فناداها﴾ refers to the angel or to Isa. It is reported from Qatada that the pronoun in "tahtiha" refers to the palm tree. Zirr and Alqama read "fakhatabaha min tahtiha" (and he addressed her from beneath her).

The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about al-sari, and he said: "It is the stream [[Reported by al-Tabarani in al-Saghir and Ibn Adi, through the narration of Abu Sinan Sa'id ibn Sinan from Abu Ishaq from al-Bara', from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His words ﴿قَدْ جَعَلَ رَبُّكِ تَحْتَكِ سَرِيًّا﴾ (﴿Your Lord has provided a stream beneath you﴾): he said, "al-sari is the river." Al-Tabarani said: no one raised it (to the Prophet) from Abu Ishaq except Abu Sinan, and Mu'awiya ibn Yahya narrated it from him, and he is weak. It was also reported by Abd al-Razzaq from al-Thawri from Abu Ishaq from al-Bara' as a statement of his own (mawquf), and likewise al-Bukhari mentioned it in suspended form (ta'liq) from Waki' from Isra'il from Abu Ishaq. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through Adam from Isra'il in the same way. al-Hakim reported it from another route from Abu Ishaq as mawquf. On this topic there is also a report from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The sari which Allah the Exalted mentioned to Maryam is a river which Allah brought forth so that she might drink from it." It was reported by al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, in the biography of Ikrima, from Ibn Umar; and a narration from Ayyub ibn Nahik, whom Abu Hatim and Abu Zur'a declared weak.]]."

Labid said:

"So they both crossed the bank of the stream and split (the water) for the two of them,
a clear spring whose surroundings were full."

[[Labid's lines: "fa-tawassata 'arda al-sari fasad'ā... masjūra mutajāwiran qallāmuhā"; "fa-mada wa-qaddamahā wa-kānat 'ādatan... minhu idhā hiya 'arrādat aqdāmuhā."

"fatawassata 'arḍa al-sarī fa-ṣadda'ā ... masjūratan mutajāwiran qallāmuhā" is from his Mu'allaqa, describing a wild donkey which went after its she-ass toward the water, while it put her in front of it. "Aqdāmuhā" is the subject of kāna, and the feminine ta' was attached to it because the feet take the feminine from the pronoun added to them. It was said: because it has the meaning of "al-taqaddima" (precedence), which is the verbal noun of "qaddamahā" (the doubled form), like "al-taqdīm." "'Āda" is the predicate of kāna. "Idhā hiya 'arradat" with doubling, meaning she delayed and became cowardly. "Fatawassatā" means the male and the female donkey, "'arḍa al-sarī" means the side and edge of the small river, "fa-ṣadda'ā" means they both split (the water) — "masjūra" means full. The noun was in the place of a pronoun, but it was made explicit so that the description could be made. Or for the sake of the comparison, or "al-ayn" is from the river, and it is not the same thing; and this is more correct. "Al-qallām" with a kasra, is al-qāqilā, and it was said it is any plant, and "tajāwuzuh" is a metaphor for its abundance.]]

It was also said: al-sari is from al-saru [[His statement "and it was said: it is from al-saru" — in al-Sihah, "al-saru" means generosity in manliness. (Ayn)]]. The intended meaning is Isa. It is reported from al-Hasan: "By Allah, he was a noble servant (abdan sariyyan)."

If you ask: was her grief over the lack of food and drink, so that she was consoled by the stream and the dates? I answer: the consolation through these two was not because they were food and drink, but because they were two miracles that show people that she is among those protected (from sin) and far from suspicion, and that the accusations they leveled against her are baseless, and that she has divine matters which are outside of ordinary custom, beyond what they were used to and accustomed to, so that it becomes clear to them that her giving birth without a father is not an unprecedented matter in her case.

Qur'an 19:25–26 is the verse-range here; the commentary passage follows.

"Tusāqiṭ" (a verb form) is read in nine ways: tusāqiṭ, with the two tāʾs assimilated (idghām); tatasāqaṭ, with both tāʾs pronounced (iẓhār); tusāqiṭ, with the second tāʾ dropped; yusāqiṭ, with a yāʾ and the tāʾ assimilated; and tasāqaṭ, tusqit, yasqut, tasquṭ and yasquṭ. In these readings the tāʾ refers to the palm tree and the yāʾ refers to the trunk. "Ruṭaban" is either a tamyīz (specification) or a direct object (mafʿūl), depending on the reading.

On al-Mubarrad: he allowed that it be governed by "huzzī" (shake), but this is not right. The bāʾ in "bi-jidhʿi al-nakhlah" (by the trunk of the palm) is redundant, for emphasis, as in His words: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ (2:195). Or it means: perform the shaking with it, as in the line:

"He wounds, at its hamstrings, with his blade" [[The explanation of this line was given earlier in volume two, page 578; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

They said: dates have been given to women after childbirth as a custom from that time, and likewise tahnīk (rubbing the newborn's palate with date). They said it was from ʿajwah (a type of date).

It was also said: nothing is better for a woman after childbirth than fresh dates, just as nothing is better for the sick than honey. And it was said: if her delivery was difficult, there was no better food for her than fresh dates.

From Ṭalḥah ibn Sulaymān: "janiyyan" with the jīm vowelled with kasra for harmony (ītibāʿ), meaning: We combined for you, in the stream and the fresh dates, two benefits: first, eating and drinking; second, consolation of the heart, since they were two miracles. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿So eat and drink and be comforted﴾ (19:26), that is, be content of soul, do not grieve, and cast off from yourself what saddens and troubles you.

It is read "waqarrī" with kasra, the dialect of Najd. "Fa-immā tarayinna" with hamza: Ibn al-Rūmī. From Abū ʿAmr: this is from the dialect of those who say "labaʾtu bi-l-ḥajj" and "ḥalaʾtu al-sawīq" (the common form being "labaytu" and "ḥalaytu al-sawīq," meaning I made it sweet) [[His words "he says labaʾtu bi-l-ḥajj and ḥalaʾtu al-sawīq", while the common form is labaytu bi-l-ḥajj and ḥalaytu al-sawīq, meaning I made it sweet. (ʿ)]], and this is due to the interchange between the hamza and the soft letter in substitution.

﴿Ṣawman﴾ means silence (ṣamtan). In the codex of ʿAbd Allah it reads ṣamtan, and it is related from Anas ibn Mālik the same. It was also said: ṣiyāman (fasting), except that they did not speak during their fasting. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the fast of silence [[I have not seen it in this form. ʿAbd al-Razzāq transmitted from the hadith of Jābir with the wording "no silence from morning until night," and in its chain is Ḥizām ibn ʿUthmān, who is weak. Abū Dāwūd has a similar report from ʿAlī. It was mentioned earlier in the commentary on Surat al-Nisāʾ.]], because it was abrogated in his community. God commanded her to vow the fast so that she would not speak with humans who were questioning her, for two reasons: first, that ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) would suffice her in speech, by which he would clear her name; second, the dislike of arguing with fools and trading words with them. There is in this that silence before a fool is obligatory. Among the most humiliated people is a fool who finds no one to ask. It was said: she informed them that she had vowed the fast by gesture.

It was also said: speaking was permitted to her: ﴿ʾinsiyyan﴾, that is, she would speak to the angels and not to humans.

Al-Fariyy: the marvel, the extraordinary. It derives from *fara al-jild* (he cut the skin), meaning to do something unprecedented.

﴿O sister of Aaron, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother unchaste.﴾ She was his sister from his father, a most excellent man among the Children of Israel. It is also said that Aaron was the brother of Moses, peace be upon them both. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "They were only referring to Aaron the Prophet."[[I have found this only in al-Tha'labi, without a chain of transmission, and al-Tabari narrated it from al-Suddi. The statement "and it is not authentic" is inaccurate, for in Muslim, al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, it is reported: "The Prophet (ﷺ) sent me to Najran. They said to me, 'Do you not read, O sister of Aaron,' while between Moses and Jesus there were as many years as God willed, and I did not know how to answer them. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said to me: 'Why did you not tell them that they used to name themselves after their prophets and their righteous predecessors?'" Al-Tabari also narrated through Ibn Sirin: "I was told that Ka'b said that God's words, O sister of Aaron, do not refer to Aaron the brother of Moses. Aisha said to him, 'You are lying.' He said to her, 'O Mother of the Believers, if the Prophet (ﷺ) said it, then he knows best; otherwise, I find six hundred years between them.'"]]

She was among his descendants in the generation of his brothers, and between her and him there were a thousand years or more. It is related from al-Suddi that she was among his descendants. The expression "O sister of Aaron" is used as one says "O brother of Hamdan," meaning "O one of them." It is also said that Aaron was a righteous or wicked man in her time, and they likened her to him, meaning: "You were among us like him in righteousness," or they reviled her by him, not intending brothers by blood. It is mentioned that when the righteous Aaron's funeral procession passed, forty thousand people followed it, all of them named Aaron, seeking blessing through him and his name. So they said: "We used to liken you to this Aaron."

Umar ibn Lajja' al-Taymi recited, ﴿your father was not a man of evil﴾. It is also said that Yusuf the carpenter carried Maryam and her son to a cave, and they remained there for forty days until she was cleansed of her postpartum bleeding. Then she came carrying him, and Jesus spoke to her on the way, saying: "O mother, rejoice, for I am the servant of God and His Messiah." When she brought him to her people, who were a family of righteous people, they wept and said that statement.[[Commentary on "until she was cleansed of her postpartum bleeding": in the Sihah, "ta'alla" means he delayed for a period, and "ta'allat al-mar'ah min nifasiha" means she became clean from her postpartum bleeding, and "ta'alla al-rajul min 'ilatihi" means he recovered from his illness. (Ayn)]]

It is also said: they intended to stone her until Jesus, peace be upon him, spoke, and they left her.

It is also said that he spoke to them with this, and then did not speak again until he reached the age at which children speak.

كانَ (kāna, "was/is") is used to express the occurrence of the content of the sentence at an indefinite past time, which can apply to both near and distant past; here it refers specifically to the near past, and the indicator of this is the structure of the speech, and that it is brought to express wonder. Another interpretation: that نُكَلِّمُ (nukallimu, "we speak to") is a narration of a past situation, meaning: how is it that a child in the cradle was known before Jesus to speak to people in past times, such that we would speak to this one?

He (Jesus) said first, "Indeed I am a servant of Allah," in refutation of the Christians' claim that "the Book" (al-Kitab) is the Gospel (al-Injil). Scholars differed about his prophethood. It was said: he was given it in his infancy; Allah perfected his intellect and made him a prophet while still a child, going by the apparent meaning of the verse.

It was also said: its meaning is that this was already decreed in His decree. Or, the one who is to come without doubt is treated as though he had already been found, blessed wherever I am, [as the Prophet ﷺ said: "...] a benefactor wherever I may be," [[It was recorded by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, in the biography of Yunus ibn Ubayd, from al-Hasan, from Abu Hurayra, with this wording and more. He said: Hushaym alone narrated it from Yunus, and from him Shu'ayb ibn Muhammad al-Kufi. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it through this route.]] It was also said: "a teacher of good."

It was read as wa-barran (and dutiful), from Abu Nuhayk: he made his very self "dutiful" because of the extreme of his devotion to his mother. Or it is governed by a verb meaning "enjoined me," namely "obliged me," since "enjoined me to prayer" and "obliged me to it" amount to the same thing.

As for "And peace is upon me" (wa-as-salamu alayya): it was said that the definite article was introduced because he was made known by the mention before it, as when you say, "A man came to us, and the man did such-and-such." The meaning: that peace which was addressed to Yahya in the three situations is addressed to me. The sound view is that this definition is an indirect allusion to a curse upon the accusers of Maryam, peace be upon her, and her enemies among the Jews. Its verification is that the article is for the category (jins), so when he says "and the category of peace is upon me exclusively," he has implicitly indicated that its opposite is upon you. Its parallel is His saying, Exalted is He: "And peace is upon those who follow the guidance" (20:47), meaning that punishment is upon those who deny and turn away; and since the setting was one of rejection and obstinacy, this is a sign of such an allusion.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 34:

Ásim and Ibn ʿĀmir read qawla l-ḥaqqi with the accusative (naṣb). It is reported from Ibn Masʿud: "qāla l-ḥaqqa" and "qāla llāh." And from al-Ḥasan: qawlu l-ḥaqqi, with a ḍamma on the qāf, and likewise in al-Anʿām, qawluhu l-ḥaqqu. Qawl (speech), qawl (speech) and qāl (speech) have the same meaning, like al-rahb, al-rahb and al-rahab (fear).

Its nominative (irfāʿ) is either as a predicate following a predicate, or as an apposition (badal), or as the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ). As for its accusative (inteṣāb): it is in the sense of praise (ʿalā l-madḥ) if it is interpreted as the Word of Allah, and it is an absolute verbal noun (maṣdar muʾakkad) emphasizing the content of the sentence if what is meant by "the word of truth" is the speech of firmness and truthfulness, as when you say: "He is the servant of Allah, truly (ḥaqqan)." And (it means) the truth, not falsehood.

Jesus was called "the Word of Allah" and "the word of truth" only because he was born solely by the word of Allah alone, namely His saying "Be" (kun), without an intermediary father. This is naming the cause by the name of the cause, as the grass is called "the sky" (al-samāʾ) and fat is called "the rain" (al-nadāʾ). It is also possible, if "the word of truth" is meant to be Jesus, that al-Ḥaqq is a name of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that it means firmness and truthfulness. His saying "about which they dispute" (alladhī fīhi yamtarūn) supports this: that is, His matter is a certain truth, and they are in doubt about it. Yamtarūn means yashukkūn (they doubt). Al-maraya is doubt. Or yatamārūn means yatalāḥūn (they quarrel), (al-tilāḥī meaning dispute, as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ). The text of al-Nasafi reads: "or yakhtalifūn (they differ), from al-irāʾ." The Jews said: "a lying sorcerer," and the Christians said: "the son of Allah and the third of three."

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (raḍiya Llāhu ʿanhu) read: tamtarūn, in the second person (ʿalā l-khiṭāb). And from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "qawla l-ḥaqqi lladhī kāna l-nāsu fīhi yamtarūn."

Al-Zamakhshari said: The Christians are refuted and rebuked by the proof that He has no offspring, and that this is something that cannot come about or be conceived by the intellect, nor is it within His power, since it is impossible and improper that His essence should be like the essence of one from whom offspring issue. Then he explained the impossibility of that by saying that He who, when He wills anything of all kinds, brings it into being by "Be," is exalted above the likeness of a begetting animal. The saying here is a metaphor (majaz), and its meaning is: His willing a thing is necessarily followed by its existence, without any delay, so this is likened to the command of a commander who is obeyed when it reaches the one commanded who complies.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 36:

The Madinan reciters and Abu 'Amr read "wa-anna" with a fatha on the hamza (أن). Its meaning is: "And because He is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him," like His saying: ﴿And the mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah﴾ [Qur'an 72:18]. Al-Astar and Abu 'Ubayd read it with a kasra, as a new sentence (ibtida'). In the reading of Ubayy (ibn Ka'b): "inna Allaha" with a kasra and without the waw, and "wa-bi-anna Allaha," meaning: "because of that," [[His saying "and because of that, namely, Allah" is perhaps meant as: "that is, because Allah." It is possible that it is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "inna Allaha," and in Ubayy's reading both readings would then be present. (ʿA) (2 - Kashshaf - 3)]] so worship Him.

The Confederates (al-Ahzab): the Jews and the Christians, according to al-Kalbi. It means that his truthfulness was extreme and that he confirmed a great deal of God's unseen matters, His signs, His books and His messengers. The predominance and emphasis of this confirmation lay in the books and the messengers. That is, he confirmed all the prophets and their books, and he was a prophet in himself, as in His saying ﴿Nay, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾ (37:37). Or it means he was eminent in truthfulness, because the foundation of prophethood is truthfulness, and one who confirms God through His signs and miracles is fit to be like this. This sentence stands as a parenthetical insertion between the substituted noun and its substitute, namely Abraham.

*Idh* (when) is like your saying "I saw Zayd" and "what a fine man your brother is." It is permissible for *idh* to be governed by *kana* (was), or by *siddiqan nabiyyan* (a truthful prophet), meaning that he combined the qualities of the truthful and the prophets when he addressed his father with those addresses.

The purpose of the Messenger's mention of him and his story in the Book is that he recite it to the people and convey it to them, as in His saying ﴿Recite to them the story of Abraham﴾ (26:69). Otherwise, God, Mighty and Majestic, is the one who mentions him and includes him in His revelation.

The *ta'* in *ya abati* (O my father) is a replacement (iwad) for the first-person possessive *ya'* (ya al-idafah). One does not say *ya abati* with the *ya'* as well, lest the replacement and the replaced be combined. It was also said: *ya abata*, because the alif is a substitute for the *ya'*. Sibawayh compared this to *aynuq* (she-camels), where the *ya'* is a compensation for the dropped waw.

Consider how he, when he wished to advise and admonish his father concerning the great error he was entangled in, and the appalling transgression by which he disobeyed the command of sensible people and departed from the principle of discernment, and the stupidity beyond which there is no stupidity: how he arranged his speech with him in the best order and delivered it in the most graceful manner, while employing courtesy, gentleness, kindness, softness, good manners and fine character, taking as his model the counsel of his Lord, Mighty and Exalted. Abu Hurayrah narrated, saying: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God revealed to Abraham, peace be upon him: 'You are My friend. Be good in your conduct, even with the disbelievers, and you will enter the places of the righteous.'" For My word has preceded for the one whose conduct is good: I will shade him beneath My Throne, settle him in the enclosure of holiness, and bring him near to My presence.

He first asked him for the cause of his error, a request that alerts him to his persistence and rouses him from his excess and extremity. For if the object of worship were living, discerning, hearing, seeing, capable of reward and punishment, benefiting and harming, yet merely one of the creatures, it would still be foolish for his worshippers to ascribe lordship to him, and it would brand him with manifest error and great injustice, even if he were the noblest of creatures and highest in rank, such as the angels and the prophets. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would He command you to disbelief after you have submitted?﴾ (3:80). This is because worship is the utmost degree of veneration, and it is due only to one who possesses the utmost bounty: the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life and death, the Rewarder and Punisher, from whom come the roots and branches of all blessings. So if it is directed to other than Him, and He is exalted far above having this attribute bestowed on another, it is nothing but injustice, transgression, error, disbelief, denial, and departure from the sound and luminous to the corrupt and dark. So what is your opinion of one who directs his worship to an inanimate stone that has no sense or perception? It does not hear your mention of it or your praise of it, nor does it see the forms of your humility and submission to it, let alone that it could help you by warding off a calamity from you, or fulfilling a need that arises for you.

Then he followed this by summoning him to the truth, showing gentleness and kindness toward him. He did not call his father ignorant in an extreme way, nor did he call himself superior in knowledge. Rather he said: "Indeed, there has come to me some knowledge and something of it that has not come to you," and that is the knowledge of guidance to the straight path. So do not be too proud. Suppose that I and you are travelling, and I have knowledge of the way that you lack, so follow me and I will save you from going astray and wandering.

Then he reinforced this by discouraging him and forbidding what he was upon: that Satan, who disobeyed your Lord, the Most Merciful, from whom all the blessings you have come, is your enemy who desires for you nothing but every ruin, disgrace and punishment, and is the enemy of your father Adam and all of your kind. It is he who has thrust you into this error, commanded you to it, and made it attractive to you. So if you examine carefully, you are worshipping Satan. However, Abraham, peace be upon him, because of his thoroughness in sincerity and the elevation of his aspiration toward the divine, mentioned from Satan's offences only those that pertain specifically to the Lord of Glory, namely his disobedience and arrogance. He did not turn to mention Satan's hostility toward Adam and his descendants, as if the consideration of the magnitude of what he had committed had overwhelmed his thought and covered his mind.

Then he finished by warning him of the evil consequence and of what his situation drags in its wake of responsibility and calamity. This did not depart from good manners, for he did not state explicitly that punishment would certainly befall him and that torment would surely cling to him. Instead he said: "I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you," so he mentioned fear and touching, and he left "punishment" indefinite. He also made Satan's guardianship and his entry into the company of his followers and allies greater than the punishment, because God's pleasure is greater than the reward itself. God, Exalted, described it as the great triumph, saying: ﴿And the pleasure of God is greater. That is the great triumph﴾ (9:72). Likewise, Satan's guardianship, which is the opposite of God's pleasure, is greater than and more grievous than the punishment itself. He opened each of the four admonitions with the words "O my father," seeking his favour and softening his heart.

*Ma* in ﴿what does not hear﴾ and ﴿what has not come to you﴾ may be a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a qualifying noun (mawsufah). The object of ﴿does not hear and does not see﴾ is left unstated and not intended, as when you say "he has no hearing and no sight." *Shay'an* (anything) has two possibilities. The first is that it occupies the position of a verbal noun, meaning "some help," and it may be understood along with the two preceding verbs. The second is that it is a direct object, from the expression "he wards off his face from me." ﴿Indeed, there has come to me some knowledge that has not come to you﴾ (19:43), in which there is a renewal of knowledge with him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 46:

When he had made him aware of the ugliness of the image of his position, and demolished his doctrine with decisive proofs, and advised him with that wondrous counsel together with those gentle words, the old man (al-Shaykh) turned on him with the coarseness of disbelief and the harshness of obstinacy. He called him by his name, and did not pair "O my father" (yā abatī) with "O my son" (yā bunayya). In his words ﴿Are you averse to my gods, O Abraham?﴾ he placed the predicate before the subject (araghibun anta ʿan ālihatī), because it was more important to him, and it was what he cared about more. In it there is a kind of wonder and denial at Abraham's aversion to his gods, and that his gods are such that no one should be averse to them. In this there is consolation and a soothing of the heart of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding what he would encounter of such things from the disbelievers of his people.

﴿Surely, if you do not desist, I will stone you﴾ (la-arjumannaka): I will strike you with my tongue, meaning insult and reproach; and from this comes "al-rajim" (the accursed one), the one pelted with curses. Or: I will kill you, from the stoning of the adulterer. Or: I will drive you away, pelting you with stones.

The root of rajm is throwing (al-ramy) with rujam, meaning large stones, as in al-Sihah.

﴿And leave me alone for a long time﴾ (malliyyan): a long time, from al-mulawah (lengthy duration). Or: "leave me for a long time, away from me and in abandonment, before I beat you severely so that you cannot move away." It is said: "So-and-so is capable of such-and-such (mallī bi-kadha)" when he is able to bear it and equal to it.

If you ask: on what is "wa-ihjurnī" (and leave me) coordinated? I say: it is coordinated with a deleted antecedent indicated by "la-arjumannaka," meaning: "so beware of me and leave me," because "la-arjumannaka" is a threat and a rebuke.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verses 47–48:

﴿Peace be upon you.﴾ This is a farewell and a parting, like His saying: ﴿To us our deeds, and to you your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek out the ignorant.﴾ (Qur'an 28:55) and His saying: ﴿When the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾ (Qur'an 25:63). This is evidence for the permissibility of parting from the one being advised when the situation is such. It is also possible that he prayed for his safety to win him over. Do you not see that he promised him forgiveness? If you ask: how was it permissible for him to ask forgiveness for a disbeliever and to promise him that?

[[Mahmud said: "If you say, why did he ask forgiveness for his father while he was a disbeliever... etc." Ahmad said: This is a remnant of Mu'tazilism, spreading sparks from the evil of the doctrine of moral goodness and badness (al-tahsin wa al-taqbih). The truth is that reason has no role in ruling on the judgment of God the Exalted before the revelation of the Law concerning it. Then al-Zamakhshari did not fulfil this, for he made reason permit seeking forgiveness and made the Law prohibit it. This cannot be conceived according to their collapsing principle, just as it cannot be conceived that the Law comes with something contrary to reason in matters of divinity. Yes, the Law may judge by what reason, in their view, does not show to be contrary. But as for what reason shows to be contrary, no.]]

I say:

They said: He meant to make repentance from disbelief a condition, just as the commands and prohibitions of the Law are directed at disbelievers while the meaning is to make faith a condition; and just as the one in a state of ritual impurity (muhdath) and the poor man are commanded to pray and to give zakat while the meaning is to make ablution and the minimum amount (nisab) a condition.

They also said: He only asked forgiveness for him by his saying: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was of the astray.﴾ (Qur'an 26:86), because he had promised him that he would believe.

They cited as evidence His saying: ﴿And the request for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him.﴾ (Qur'an 9:114).

And one may say: What prevented seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever is revelation (al-sam'), but as for the rational matter, it does not forbid it. So it is permissible that the promise of forgiveness and its fulfilment occurred before the revelation arrived, based on the rational judgment. What indicates its soundness is His saying: ﴿except the saying of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you"﴾ (Qur'an 60:4). Had it been a condition of faith, it would not have been reprehensible and an exception to what made the following of him obligatory. As for ﴿because of a promise he had made to him﴾, the one who promised is Abraham, not Azar. That is, he did not say ﴿And forgive my father﴾ except from his saying ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you.﴾ And the reading of Hammad al-Riwaya supports this: "wa'adaha abahu" (he promised it to his father).

And God knows best.

﴿Affectionate (hafiyyan)﴾: al-Hafiyy is one who is exceedingly kind and gentle. One says: hafiya bihi and tahaffa bihi.

﴿And I will withdraw from you﴾: by withdrawal he meant emigration to Syria. The meaning of "supplication" (al-du'a') is worship, because it is part of worship and among its means. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Supplication is worship."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud and the rest of the authors of the Sunan, and Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir. It was also narrated by Ahmad, Ishaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Ya'la, al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabari from his hadith, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] And His saying supports it: ﴿So when he withdrew from them and from what they worshipped besides Allah﴾ (Qur'an 19:49). He alluded to their wretchedness by the supplication to their gods in His saying: ﴿Perhaps I shall not be, in the supplication to my Lord, unfortunate﴾ (Qur'an 19:48; cf. 19:48 as quoted in al-Shu'ara' context), together with humility before God through the word "perhaps" (ʿasā) and what it contains of self-abasement.

Nobody has lost anything with Allah by abandoning the disbelievers and the sinners for His sake. Allah compensates him with believing children who are prophets, ﴿and We bestowed upon them of Our mercy﴾, which is prophethood, according to al-Hasan. According to al-Kalbi, it means wealth and children, and it is general to every good, religious and worldly, that they were given.

﴿And grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ means a good reputation. He expressed by "tongue" what exists through the tongue, just as he expressed by "hand" what is said of the hand, which is a gift. The poet said:

"Indeed there came to me a tongue with which I am not delighted, from the heights (of Najd), with neither a lie in it nor sorcery.
So the soul surged (ferment) when it came to them, and a rider came from Thalith, a visitor."

He made the verb feminine by interpreting the agent as "word" or "message," and mentioned it masculine afterward, considering the apparent form. "Min 'uluw" is with the ending on fatḥah, meaning: from the highest part of Najd. "Al-Sakhar" is the verbal noun of sakhara, like ta'iba. "Jashat al-qidr" means the pot boiled and what was in it rose up. Figurative use of "jayashan" for the heat of the heart is well known. "Al-Fulla" means a group. "Thalith" is a place name, not subject to nunation (diptote). "Rakib" is coordinated with "fa-lahum," "mu'tamir" is its adjective, and "jaa" the second is a substitute (badal).

He gave that to his descendants, so He exalted their mention and praised them, just as He exalted his mention and praised him.

Al-Rasul (the messenger): one who has a book with him from among the prophets. Al-Nabi (the prophet): one who gives news from God, Mighty and Majestic, even if he does not have a book with him, like Yusha' (Joshua).

The right side (al-Ayman) of the mountain, meaning from its right-hand side. Or "from the right" (min al-yaman) is an adjective qualifying al-Tur, or qualifying al-Janib (the side). He is likened to one whom some great figures brought near for intimate conversation, when He spoke to him without an intermediary angel. It is narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah that He brought him so close that he heard the scratching (sarif) of the pen with which the Torah was written.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 53:

"[We granted him] out of Our mercy" — that is, because of Our mercy toward him and Our compassion for him: We bestowed upon him Harun. Or [it means] "some of Our mercy," as in His words ﴿And We gave them of Our mercy﴾. And "his brother" in this reading is in apposition (badal), and "Harun" is an explicative apposition ('atf bayan), like your saying: "I saw a man, your brother Zayd." Harun was older than Musa, so the bestowal was on his support and his backing (of Musa). This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verses 54–55:

Ismail (peace be upon him) is mentioned for his truthfulness in promise, although this quality is found in other prophets as well, as an honour and a mark of distinction for him, like the epithets al-Halim (the Forbearing), al-Awwah (the Sorrowful and Supplicating), and al-Siddiq (the Truthful). It is also because it is the most well-known and most often described of his qualities. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he promised a companion of his that he would wait for him at a place, and he waited for him a year. And it is enough that he promised himself patience in the face of slaughter, and he fulfilled it, when he said: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient﴾. He used to begin with his family in commanding righteousness and worship, so that he might make them an example for those behind them, and because they have more right than other people: ﴿And warn your nearest kindred﴾, and ﴿Enjoin prayer upon your family﴾, and ﴿Save yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾. Do you not see that they have the greater claim to be given charity to, so religious benevolence is more fitting for them? It was also said that "his family" means his whole community, both kin and others, because the peoples of the prophets are counted among their households. And in this is the lesson that it is the right of the righteous person not to spare sincere counsel to strangers, let alone relatives and those connected to him, and to enrich them with religious benefits and not to neglect any of that.
