Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 58:

﴿Those﴾ refers to those mentioned in the surah, from Zakariyya to Idris, peace be upon him. The ﴿min﴾ in ﴿of the prophets﴾ is explanatory (bayan), like its use in His saying, exalted is He, at the end of Surat al-Fath: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds among them forgiveness﴾, because all the prophets are blessed. The second ﴿min﴾, in ﴿of those whom We guided﴾, is partitive (tab'id). Idris was of the offspring of Adam, being close to him, for he was the grandfather of the father of Nuh. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was of the offspring of those who were carried with Nuh:

because he was of the offspring of Sam ibn Nuh; and Isma'il was of the offspring of Ibrahim. Musa, Harun, Zakariyya and Yahya were of the offspring of Isra'il. Likewise Isa, because Maryam was of his offspring. ﴿And of those whom We guided﴾ may be understood as conjoined to the first and the second ﴿min﴾. If you make ﴿those﴾ the predicate of ﴿those﴾ [i.e. the subject], then ﴿when the revelations of the Most Merciful are recited to them﴾ is a resumed (mustanaf) sentence. If you make it a qualifier of it, then it is the predicate. Shibl ibn 'Abbad al-Makki recited ﴿yutla﴾ with the masculine form, because the feminine is not real when a separator intervenes. ﴿Bukiyy﴾ is the plural of ﴿baki﴾ (weeping), like ﴿sujjad﴾ and ﴿qu'ud﴾ in the plurals of ﴿sajid﴾ and ﴿qa'id﴾. From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Recite the Qur'an and weep; and if you do not weep, then feign weeping [[Narrated by Ishaq and al-Bazzar through the route of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Mulayka, from Ibn Abi Mulayka, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id, with the wording "Indeed this Qur'an was revealed with sorrow, so when you recite it, weep; and if you do not weep, then feign weeping – the hadith." It was also narrated by Abu Ya'la and al-Harith through this route, and by al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab. Isma'il [i.e. one of the transmitters] is also weak.]]" And from Salih al-Murri, may Allah be pleased with him: "I recited the Qur'an to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a dream, and he said to me: 'This is the recitation, O Salih, so where is the weeping?'" And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "When you recite the prostration of Surat Subhan, do not hurry to prostrate until you weep; and if the eye of one of you does not weep, then let his heart weep." And from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Indeed the Qur'an was revealed with sorrow, so when you recite it, be sorrowful [[Narrated by Ibn Mardawayh from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas with the wording "so recite it with sorrow," and its chain is weak. Abu Ya'la and al-Uqayli narrated it, and Abu Nu'aym in the biography of Rabah ibn 'Amr al-'Absi from the hadith of Abu Burayda from his father with the wording "Recite the Qur'an with sorrow, for it was revealed with sorrow."]]" And they said: in the prostration of recitation one supplicates with what befits its verse. So if one recites the verse of the prostration in Surat al-Sajda, he says: "O Allah, make me among those who prostrate to Your face, who glorify You with Your praise, and I seek refuge in You from being among those who are arrogant towards Your command." And if he recites the prostration of Surat Subhan, he says: "O Allah, make me among those who weep towards You and are humbled before You." And if he recites this [verse], he says: "O Allah, make me among Your servants upon whom You have bestowed favour, those guided, who prostrate to You, and who weep at the recitation of Your verses."

**Khalafahu:** if it came after him (i.e., his successor, offspring). The word *khalf* with a fatha is used for what follows something good, and *khalf* with a sukun for what follows something bad, just as they say *wa'd* (promise) for the guarantee of good and *wa'id* (threat) for the guarantee of evil. From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: they are the Jews, who abandoned the obligatory prayer, drank wine, and made lawful marriage to a sister from the father's side.

From Ibrahim and Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with them both: they neglected it by delaying it. The first interpretation is supported by His saying ﴿except for one who repents, believes﴾, meaning the disbelievers. From Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, on His saying ﴿and followed their desires﴾: [they were people who] built lofty buildings, rode conspicuous mounts, and wore famous clothing. From Qatadah, may Allah be pleased with him: it refers to this community. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak, may Allah be pleased with them, read *al-salawat* (the prayers) in the plural.

Among the Arabs, every evil is *ghayy* (error), and every good is *rushad* (right guidance). Al-Murraqqish said:

*"Whoever meets with good, people praise his affair,
and whoever goes astray will not lack someone blaming him for his error."*

[[*"Do you sit up in the morning, scratching the ground, pensive and grieving, from a dream? Dreams may overcome one who was sleeping,"*

*"Whoever meets with good, people praise his affair, and whoever goes astray will not lack someone blaming him for his error."*

This is by al-Murraqqish al-Asghar, the companion of Fatimah bint al-Mundhir; al-Akbar was the uncle of al-Asghar and the uncle of Tarafah, and he was the companion of Asma'. The interrogative is for reproach. *Al-hulm* (with two dammahs) is what the sleeper sees. *Al-nakt* is drawing lines and tapping the ground with a finger or a stick, as the troubled and reflective person does. *Al-wajim* is the grieving one; the *waw* is for the circumstantial clause, meaning: while the confused dreams may overcome the sleeper, so that it is devoid of meaning. "Whoever meets" means whoever encounters good in his actions; people praise his deed or his condition, and the praise is attached to it because it is its cause. Whoever commits error will not lack someone to blame him for his error. It is also said that by "good" he meant wealth and by "poverty" he meant... but this is distant, given the context of blame and its lack of fit with what precedes it. *Ghawa yaghwa* (of the *darab* pattern) means to be immersed in ignorance; *adama ya'damu* (of the *ʿalima* pattern) means to lack, to be deprived of.]]

From al-Zajjaj: it is the recompense of *ghayy*, like His saying ﴿will meet with a penalty (athama)﴾, meaning the recompense of *athām*. Or *ghayy* means deviation from the path of Paradise.

It is also said that *ghayy* is a valley in Hell from which its other valleys seek refuge. Al-Akhfash read *yulqūna* (they will be met).

Read as "yudkhalūna" and "yudkhalūna" (both forms are recited): meaning they will not be deprived of any part of the reward for their deeds, nor will it be withheld from them; rather, it will be multiplied for them, clarifying that the prior disbelief does not harm them if they repent of it. This is like your saying: "What prevented you (mā ẓalamaka) from doing such-and-such," meaning: "What prevented you." Or, it means they will not be wronged at all, not even a little of wrongdoing.

Since Paradise contains the Gardens of Eden, the phrase is put in apposition (badal) to it, as when you say: "I saw your house, the hall and the upper rooms." "Adn" is a proper noun (ism 'alam) meaning "residence" (al-'adn, i.e., al-iqamah), just as they made fayna, sahr and amsi, when not declined (ghayr munsarif), proper nouns for the senses of "the time," "the pre-dawn," and "yesterday." Thus 'adn is treated like these words on that basis.

[[The author's words "li-ma'ani al-fayna" [in the sense of "al-fayna"]: In al-Sihah: "I met him fayna ba'da fayna," meaning "from time to time." If you wish, you may drop the alif and lam and say: "I met him fayna," just as they said "laqituhu al-undara" and "undara." (Ibn al-Munir/editor's gloss.)]] as well as sahr and amsi, so it follows the pattern of 'adn for this reason.

Or it is a proper name for the land of Paradise, because it is a place of residence. Were it not so, the substitution would not be permissible, since an indefinite noun may only substitute for a definite one when it is qualified, and it would not be permissible to describe it with "allati" (which).

It is also read as "jannati 'adn" and "jannatu 'adn" in the nominative, as a subject (mubtada'). That is: He promised it while it is unseen by them and not present. Or they are absent from it and do not witness it. Or [the meaning is] the affirmation of the unseen and belief in it.

It has been said that in "ma'tiyyan" the form is a passive participle (maf'ul) used in the sense of an active participle (fa'il).

The better view is that the promise is Paradise itself, and they come to it. Or it is from your saying: "He came to him in kindness" (atā ilayhi ihsanan), meaning: his promise was a fulfilled, accomplished thing.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 62:

Al-lagw (لغو): superfluous speech and that which has no benefit in it. Here is a clear indication of the obligation to avoid idle talk (lagw) and guard against it, in that God has exalted the Abode in which there is no obligation (taklif) from it. How beautiful is His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿When they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity. And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say: "For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant."﴾ We seek refuge in God from idle talk, ignorance, and plunging into what does not concern us. That is: if the greeting of some of them to one another, or the greeting of the angels to them, is idle talk, then they hear no idle talk except that. It is of the same type as his saying:

"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords, by them, are notched from the clashing of battalions."

[[The explanation of this verse has been given earlier on page 142 of the second volume, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector (muṣahhih) says: end.]]

Or they hear therein only a saying in which they are free from fault and defect, as a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati').

[[Mahmud said: "It is permissible that it be from his saying:

'And there is no fault in them, except that their swords, by them, are notched from the clashing of battalions,'

and that it be a disjunctive exception." Ahmad said: The difference between the two aspects is that he made the notching (fulul) a fault by way of metaphor (tajawwuz), in order to negate fault entirely, as if he were saying: "If the notching of swords from clashing is a fault, then they are people with a fault," meaning: and if it is not a fault, then there is absolutely no fault in them, for there is nothing other than this. So, after this metaphor and supposition, it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil).]]

Or because the meaning of salam (سلام) is the supplication for safety.

[[His words resume. He said: "It is also permissible that it be connected, with salam being the supplication for safety ... etc." Ahmad said: This makes it a connected exception according to the原 literal sense, unlike the first, which arises from metaphor. Yet this is still distant, because it requires the affirmation that idle talk and superfluity are heard in Paradise, and God forbid, for there is no nonsense (ghawl) in it and no idle talk.]]

The Abode of Peace (dar al-salam) is the abode of safety, and its people are free from supplication for safety. So its outward meaning would fall under idle talk and superfluous speech, were it not for the benefit of honour (ikram) in it.

Among people is one who eats a single meal (wajbah) [[His words "one who eats a single meal (al-wajbah)" mean one who eats once a day and night, and one has made oneself eat once (wajjaba nafsahu tawjiban) when one accustoms it to that, as in the Sihah. (Ṭ)]]. And among them is one who eats whenever he finds food, and this is the habit of the greedy (al-manhumin).

And among them is one who takes a midday meal and an evening meal, and this is the moderate, praiseworthy habit. There is no night or day there, but this is by way of estimation, and because the one who is pampered among the Arabs is one who finds a midday meal and an evening meal. It was said: he meant the continuity and abundance of provision, as you say: "I am with so-and-so morning and evening, and early and late," meaning constancy, and you do not intend the two known times.

nuwrithu. It is also read as nuwarrithu (intensive form), a metaphor (istiʿara): meaning, We leave the Garden to them as one leaves an inheritance to the heir from the estate of the deceased. Also, because the pious meet their Lord on the Day of Resurrection with their deeds concluded while their fruit remains, namely the Garden, when He admits them into the Garden He has indeed made them inheritors of their piety, just as an heir inherits property from the one who has died. It is also said: they inherit from the Garden the dwellings that were meant for the people of the Fire had they obeyed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 64:

﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord.﴾ This is a quotation of the words of Jibril (peace be upon him), when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was slow to receive revelation from him. It is narrated that he was delayed for forty days. It is also said: fifteen days. This was when he was asked about the story of the People of the Cave, Dhu al-Qarnayn, and the Spirit, and he did not know how to answer, and he hoped that revelation would come to him concerning it. This grieved him greatly, and the polytheists said: "His Lord has abandoned him and become averse to him." When Jibril (peace be upon him) descended, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "You were late, until my suspicion grew and I longed for you." He said: "I was more eager than you, but I am a servant under command. When I am sent, I descend, and when I am held back, I am held back." Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed this verse and Surat al-Duha.

It is a verbal noun of "nazala," and "nazala" can mean "anzala" (to cause to descend), and it can mean gradual descent. The fitting meaning here is descent at intervals. The meaning is that our descent at times, moment after moment, is only by the command of Allah and according to what He sees as right and wise. To Him belongs what is before us, *wa ma khalfana* (what is behind us), and *wa ma bayna dhalika* (what is between that), i.e., the directions and places and what is between them. We cannot move from one direction to another or from one place to another except by the command and will of the Sovereign. He is the Guardian, knowing every movement and stillness, and what occurs and renews of conditions. Heedlessness and forgetfulness are not permissible for Him. How, then, can we move about in His dominion unless He sees it as a benefit and wisdom, and grants us permission for it?

It is also said: "What is past of the affairs of this world, and what is yet to come of the affairs of the Hereafter, and what is between them is what is between the two blasts, which is forty years." It is also said: "What has passed of our lives, what remains of them, and the state we are in." It is also said: "What is before our existence and what is after our annihilation." It is also said: "The earth that is before us when we descend, the sky that is behind us, and what is between the sky and the earth." The meaning is that He encompasses everything; nothing is hidden from Him, and not an atom's weight escapes Him. So how should we proceed to an act we initiate except as proceeding from what His wisdom requires, what He commands us, and what He permits us?

It is also said that the meaning of *wa ma kana rabbuka nasiyya* is: "and your Lord was not one who abandons you," as in His saying, Exalted is He: *ma wadda'aka rabbuka wa ma qala* (your Lord has not abandoned you, nor has He become averse). That is, the prevention of descent was only due to the prevention of the command to it. As for the delay of revelation, it was not from God's abandoning you or leaving you, but because it depends on a benefit.

It is also said: this is a quotation of the words of the righteous when they enter Paradise, meaning: "We do not enter Paradise except that Allah has bestowed favour upon us for the reward of our deeds and commanded us to enter it." He is the Owner of the reins of all affairs, past, anticipated, and present, the Gentle in the works of goodness, the Enabler of them, and the Rewarder for them. Then Allah, exalted, said, affirming their words: *wa ma kana rabbuka nasiyya*: "your Lord is not forgetful of the works of those who labour, nor heedless of what they ought to be rewarded for." And how is forgetfulness or heedlessness permissible for the Possessor of the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them?

Then He said to His Messenger (ﷺ): "Since you have come to know Him with these attributes, then turn to the work and worship Him, and He will reward you as He rewards others of the righteous."

Al-Aʿraj (may Allah be pleased with him) recited: *wa ma yatanazzalu*, with the ya', as a quotation about Jibril (peace be upon him), with the pronoun referring to the revelation.

And it is related from Ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with him): *illa bi-qawli rabbika* (except by the word of your Lord). The disagreement regarding *nasiyya* must be like that regarding *baghiyya*.

**Rabbu l-samawati wa l-ard** (the Lord of the heavens and the earth) is a *badal* (substitute or apposition) for *rabbika* (your Lord). It may also be the *khabar* (predicate) of an omitted *mubtada'* (subject), meaning: "He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." So: **﴿fa-'budhu﴾** (so worship Him), as in the verse of the poet:

*And a speaker from Khawlan said: "Marry their young woman,*
*and the most honored of the two clans is unmarried, as she was."*

The poet is unknown; the meaning is "and [many is] the speaker." Khawlan, with a fatḥah on the kh, is the name of a tribe in Yemen. It is the *mubtada'*, and its predicate is what follows it. The *fa'* in *fa-nkiḥ* is extra (*za'idah*) according to al-Akhfash and al-Farra', while Sibawayh rejected its being extra here, because the *mubtada'* does not resemble a conditional. So the predicate is omitted: "Khawlan are noble; so marry their young woman," meaning, "marry their young woman." Alternatively, it is the predicate of an omitted subject: "These are Khawlan, known for generosity, so marry their young woman."

**Akrūmat** is formed from *al-karam* (generosity) to indicate abundance of generosity, just as **a'jūbah** is formed from *al-ta'ajjub* (wonder) to indicate its abundance. The clause is a *ḥāliyyah* (circumstantial clause). It may prevent marrying the young woman: she said this to me, while the most honored of the two clans, meaning the most honored of my father's clan and my mother's clan, is **khalw** (with a ḍammah), empty of spouses as she was, so she has more right than the young woman to marriage because of her kinship to me. It may also be encouraging him to marry: she said this while the young woman, who is the most honored of the two clans, namely her father's clan and her mother's clan, from Khawlan, remains a virgin, or unmarried, and has not married anyone before me. So she deserves to be married by me because both her sides are noble. Thus the **kāf** here means **'alā** ("upon"). It is also possible that her present state is compared with her past state, in which case the **kāf** keeps its original meaning of resemblance. It is also possible that the **wāw** is conjunctive: she said that, and she said that she is unmarried, untouched by anyone before you, so she deserves marriage for that reason. But this is far-fetched.

On this interpretation, **﴿wa-mā kāna rabbuka nasiyyā﴾** (and your Lord was never forgetful) may be the words of the righteous, and what follows is the words of the Lord of Majesty.

If you ask: why did He not use **iṣṭabir** with **'alā**, the complement that goes with it, as in **﴿wa-ṣṭabir 'alayhā﴾** (and be patient over it)?

The answer: because worship has been treated as if it were the opponent (*qarn*) in your saying to a warrior, "iṣṭabir li-qirnika" (stand firm against your opponent), meaning: stand firm against him in the hardships that he brings upon you. The meaning is that worship brings upon you hardships and difficulties, so stand firm for it and do not weaken, and do not let your chest be constricted by your enemies among the People of the Book throwing their falsehoods at you, or by the delay of revelation for a period, or by the mockery of the polytheists at you.

**Lam yusamma shay'un bi-llāh qaṭṭ**: No one was ever named with Allah. They used to call their idols "gods" (*ālihah*), and they said "al-'Uzzā is a god" (*ilāh*). As for the one in which the **alif** and **lām** replaced the **hamzah**, it is specific to the true object of worship, without any partner in it.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that no one is named al-Raḥmān except Him.

Another interpretation: do you know anyone named with His name in truth rather than falsehood? Because naming in falsehood, since it is not counted, is as if there were no naming at all. It was said:

*"a peer and an equal."*

That is, if it is established that there is no deity to whom the servants direct worship except Him alone, then there is no escape from worshipping Him and being patient with its burdens and obligations.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verses 66–67:

It is possible that by "man" (al-insan) is meant the whole human species, and it is possible that by it is meant part of the species, namely the disbelievers. If you say: why is it permissible to intend all humans, when not all of them say this? I say: since this statement exists in some of their own kind, it is valid to attribute it to all of them, as they say: "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," when the killer was in fact only one man from among them. al-Farazdaq said:

"So the sword of the Banu 'Abs, with which they struck, / Missed my hands and the head of Khalid, [Warqa's blow]."

[[This is al-Farazdaq's epithet; his name is Hammam or Humayn. He means Warqa ibn Zuhayr ibn Judhayma al-'Absi. Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik ordered him to strike the necks of some Byzantine captives and gave him a sword that could not cut. He said: "Rather, I will strike them with the sword of Abu Raghwan Mujashi'," meaning himself. He struck the neck of Khalid, the sword turned aside and slipped from the target, and they laughed at him. The sword and the striking were attributed to the Banu 'Abs although they belonged to one man of them, in honour and magnification of both. Placing it "in the hands" indicates that he was resolute in his affair, firm in his determination, not negligent.

The meaning is that caution does not avail against decree, as happened to Warqa, despite his utmost care, especially before the king. It is also permissible that the poet intends to disparage the Banu 'Abs.]]

So the striking is attributed to the Banu 'Abs, while the poet says "the sword missed the hands of Warqa," and Warqa was Warqa ibn Zuhayr ibn Judhayma al-'Absi.

If you say: with what is idha (when) in the accusative, and its government by akhraju is impossible because of the lam (of emphasis)? You would not say: "Today Zayd is standing"? I say: it is governed by a hidden verb indicated by what is mentioned. If you say: the lam of the beginning entering upon the present tense gives the meaning of the present, so how can it be combined with the particle of the future? [[Mahmud said: "If you say how the lam, which denotes the present, is combined with the particle of the future..." etc. Ahmad said:

Because of the belief that the two particles contradict, the Kufans forbade their combination. The lam was stripped of its meaning so as to suit sawfa, rather than sawfa being stripped so as to suit the lam, because if this were reversed, sawfa would be made void, since it has no meaning other than the future. As for the lam, when it is stripped of the present, the emphasis remains for it, so it is not made void, and so it is determined. And God knows best.]] I say: it is combined only in its sense of emphasis, just as the hamza is made sincere in "ya Allah" as a compensation, and the meaning of definiteness has faded from it. And "ma" in "idha ma" is also for emphasis. So it is as if they said:

"Is it true that we shall be brought out alive when death and destruction have settled among us?" in a manner of denial and disbelief.

What is meant is coming out from the earth, or from the state of annihilation. Or it is from their saying: "So-and-so came out a scholar" and "came out a brave man," when he is rare in that respect; the meaning is: "I shall come out alive, a rarity, by way of mockery." al-Hasan and Abu Haywa read: "la-sawfa akhruju." And from Talha ibn Musarrif, may Allah be pleased with him: "la-sa-akhruju," like the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "wa-la-sa-yu'tika." The placing of the adverbial phrase and its following the particle of denial is because what comes after death is the time when life is denied, and from this their denial came. It is like your saying to one who wrongs a benefactor: "When the favour of so-and-so has been bestowed upon you, do you wrong him?" The waw is a conjunction for "la yadhkuru" over "yaqulu," and the hamza of denial is placed between the conjoined and the conjunction. The meaning: does he say that and not remember the state of the first creation, so that he does not deny the second?

[[Mahmud said: "God mentioned to man the first creation so that he would acknowledge the second..." etc. Ahmad said: The doctrine of the people of the Sunna is that re-creating what has ceased to exist is rationally possible and has occurred by transmission. The creed of the people of the Sunna is the one that agrees with the verse, because the first creation was not preceded by existence, and the thing created initially was not anything before that. As for the second creation, existence preceded it, and the created thing before it was something during the time of its existence, then it ceased and its thingness was annulled. Thus the difference between the two creations is evident, as the Qur'an declares. As for the Mu'tazila: if they say that God annihilates bodies and then brings them back, they have spoken the truth, but their principle does not yield a difference between the two creations, because the non-existent in both was something before the creation. If they say bodies are not annihilated, but are scattered and then gathered, as al-Zamakhshari stated explicitly, that is because he perceived that saying bodies are annihilated and then God makes them exist, together with saying the non-existent is a thing, nullifies the difference between the two creations, and he could not bear that. The Qur'an has declared it, so he committed to the view that bodies are not annihilated, in order that the difference between the second creation (which on this account is only the gathering and assembling of existing things) and the first creation (which is the bringing into existence of the non-existent) be secured. As for the second, its counterpart has preceded it, and it returns to it like a pattern followed. There is in it only the composition of existing, remaining parts and their assembly, and returning them to what they were, gathered after disintegration and dispersal. God's saying "and he was nothing" is evidence for this meaning, and likewise His saying "and it is easier for Him." This shows that for the Lord of Might both creations are equal; difficulty and ease do not differ for His power, and He needs no imitation of a pattern, no aid from a wise one, and no consideration of a measure. Rather, He confronts the denier of resurrection with this as a repulsion in the sea of his obstinacy, and a disclosure of the page of his ignorance.

All the readers read "la yadhkuru" with the lightened form, except Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, may Allah be pleased with them, who read it with shadda ("yadhdhakkaru"), and so they lightened it [as in the text]. In the codex of Ubayy: "yatadhakkaru." "Min qablu" means: from before the state in which he is, and that state is his existence.

In Allah's swearing by His name, may His names be sanctified, when it is attributed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, there is a magnification of the Messenger's status and an elevation of it, just as He elevated the status of the heaven and the earth in His saying, ﴿So by the Lord of the heavens and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾ [51:23]. The "wa" in ﴿and the devils﴾ [19:68] may be conjunctive, and in the sense of "with" (ma'a), and "with" is more precise here. The meaning is that they will be gathered together with their companions from the devils who led them astray, each disbeliever being bound in a chain with a devil. If you say: this holds if by "man" (al-insan) only the disbelievers are meant, but if the humans in general are meant [[His words: "And 'man' may be understood to mean the generality ... etc." Ahmad (ibn al-Munayyir) said: He confused the intention of generality with the encompassing of generality, and there is a great difference between them. He stated explicitly that Allah intended by "man" the generality, and the meaning of intending the generality is that Allah intends to attribute the word of doubt and disbelief to every individual of mankind, which is far from God's protection. Al-Zamakhshari himself stated that the one who utters the word of doubt is a part of the species, so the expression is flawed, as you see. The correct expression would be: it may be that the definiteness is generic, in which case it becomes specific (ahdi), and the wording is then specific from the first moment. And Allah knows best.]], then how does their being gathered with the devils hold? I say: when all people are gathered in a single gathering, and among them the disbelievers are linked with the devils, then they have been gathered with the devils just as they have been gathered with the disbelievers.

If you say: why not separate the blessed from the wretched in the gathering, as they are separated in the recompense? I say: He does not distinguish between them in the place of gathering. They are brought to the place where they kneel around Hell, and they are brought along with the Fire, so that the blessed may witness the states from which Allah saved and delivered them, so that they increase in joy upon joy and delight upon delight, and so that they may gloat over the enemies of Allah and their own enemies. Thus their distress and regret increase, along with what enrages them of the happiness of the friends of Allah and their gloating over them. If you say: what is the meaning of bringing them kneeling (jithiyyan)? I say: as for when "man" is explained specifically, the meaning is that they are dragged (yuqbalun) from the gathering to the shore of Hell as "utullan" [[His words "utullan": al-Utull is violent dragging. This is what the Sihah states.]] in the state they were in at the place of standing, kneeling on their knees, not walking on their feet. This is because the people of the place of standing were described as kneeling. That is, their coming to it was obligatory upon Allah; He made it binding upon Himself, decreed it, and resolved that it should be otherwise. [It is] read as nunajji and nunjji, and as yunjā and yunja, in the passive form. If the whole of mankind is meant, it is clear. If only the disbelievers are meant, then the meaning of ﴿Then We will deliver those who were righteous﴾ [ثُمَّ نُنَجِّي الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا] is that the God-fearing are led to Paradise immediately after the disbelievers' wurud, not that they come to them and then escape. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, al-Jahdari and Ibn Abi Layla: thumma nanja, with the tha' fathah, meaning "there" [i.e., "thumma" as "there"]. And His saying, ﴿And We will leave the wrongdoers therein, kneeling﴾ [وَنَذَرُ الظَّالِمِينَ فِيهَا جِثِيًّا], is evidence that the meaning of wurud is kneeling around it, and that the believers part from the disbelievers toward Paradise after their kneeling, while the disbelievers remain in their place, kneeling.

Clear (bayyinat), with well-arranged wording, summarized meanings, and manifest purposes. They are either muhkamat (clear, unambiguous verses) or mutashabihat (ambiguous verses), and the clarification of the mutashabihat has been followed by the clear verses. Or they are clarified by the Messenger, in word or deed. Or they are manifestly inimitable (i'jaz), so that he challenged with them and no one could match them. Or they are proofs and demonstrations. The preferred reading is that they are a circumstantial qualifier emphasizing the sense, حالا مؤكدة (ḥālan mu'akkidatan, an emphatic circumstantial clause), as in His saying ﴿And it is the truth, confirming what is with them﴾, because the signs of God are only ever clear. And they are proofs for those who believe (lilladhina amanu). It is possible that the believers are being addressed directly, and that the unbelievers speak this way to them, and that they say it on their account and with that meaning, as in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed: "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it."﴾

Ibn Kathir recited مَقاماً (maqaman) with a ḍamma, meaning the place of residence and dwelling. The rest read it with a fatḥa, meaning the place of standing, and the intended meaning is a place or location.

Al-nadiyy: the assembly, the gathering place of the people, and where they convene (ḥaythu yantadun). [[The saying "ḥaythu yantadun" in al-Sihah: "nadawtu" means I attended the nadi (assembly). "Intadaytu" has the same meaning. (ʿ)]] The meaning is: when they hear the verses, and they are ignorant, knowing only the outward aspect of the worldly life, and that is the extent of their knowledge, they say: "Which of the two groups, the believers in the signs or those who deny them, has the greater share of this world, so that this should be taken as a measure of excellence and deficiency, of exaltation and lowliness?" It is narrated that they would comb their hair, anoint themselves with oil, perfume themselves, and adorn themselves with splendid finery, and then they would boast, claiming to be more honored by God than the poor Muslims.

Kam is the object of ahlakna (We destroyed), and min is explanatory (tabyin) of its vagueness, meaning: many generations (qurun) We destroyed.

Every people of an age is a qarn (generation) for those who come after them, because they precede them. Hum (they) is in the accusative position as a descriptive modifier (sifah) of kam. Do you not see that if you omitted hum, you would have no alternative but to put ahsan in the accusative as a descriptor?

Al-athath: the household goods (mata' al-bayt). It was also said: it is what is valuable of the furnishings. Al-khurthi: what is not of that kind. Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Tusi recited:

"Time has aged our meeting with Umm al-Walid, a long age,
and the household goods have become worn and old."

[The athath of the house are its belongings and necessities. Al-khurthi, like al-kursi, is the old of those things. He says: our meeting with Umm al-Walid has grown long and distant, that is, its time has been far apart. Dahran is a specification (tamyiz). It is also permissible that it is an adverb of time, meaning: the age of our meeting with my beloved has been far apart for a long time, and the household goods have become old and ancient. In it there is a lament over the absence of meeting.]

It is read in five ways: ri'yan, which means the appearance and form, a verbal noun in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), from ra'aytu (I saw). Ri'ian, with metathesis (qalb), like their saying ra' for ra'y. Riyan, with the hamza changed to a yaa and assimilation (idgham). Or it derives from al-riyy, which is comfort and affluence, from their saying: rayyan min al-na'im (saturated with blessings). Riya, with the hamza entirely dropped, and its basis is that the metathesized form, which is rienan, is lightened by dropping its hamza and placing its vowel on the preceding quiescent yaa. Ziyan, derived from al-ziyy, which is gathering, because al-ziyy is gathered beauties; the meaning is: better than these.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 75:

Meaning: "Let the Most Merciful extend it for him" — that is, He grants him respite and gives him time in his life. It is phrased in the form of a command to signal that this is obligatory and that it will certainly come to pass, like the commanded act that is carried out. This is so that the excuses of the misguided are cut off, and it will be said to him on the Day of Resurrection: "Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would take heed to take heed therein?" Or it is like His saying, Exalted is He: "We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin" (3:178). Or "Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend it for him, an extension" is in the sense of a supplication: that Allah grant him respite and prolong the span of his life.

In this verse there are two views. The first: that it is connected to the verse that is its fourth, and the two verses are a parenthetical interjection between them. That is, they said: "Which of the two groups is better in station and finer in assembly?" (19:73). "Until, when they see what they are promised" (19:75), meaning: they will not cease saying this statement and boasting about it, not refraining from it until they witness the promised thing with their own eyes — "either the punishment" in this world, which is the Muslims' triumph over them and their punishment of them by killing and capture, and Allah's manifesting His religion over all religions at their hands; "or the Hour" and what they will suffer of disgrace and chastisement on the Day of Resurrection. Then, at the moment of seeing it, they will know that the matter is the reverse of what they had estimated, that they are worse in place and weaker in troops, not better in station and finer in assembly, and that the believers are contrary to their description.

The second: that it is connected to what follows it. The meaning: those who are in error are granted an extension in their error. Abandonment (al-khudhlan) clings to them because of Allah's knowledge of them, and because the divine kindnesses do not benefit them and they are not among its people. What is meant by "error" is the ignorance and extremity in their disbelief that led them to the statement they made. They will not be separated from their error until they witness Allah's support of the believers or see the Hour and its precursors. If you say: what is "until" (hatta) here? I say: it is the one after which sentences are narrated. Do you not see that the conditional sentence follows it, which is His saying: "When they see what they are promised, then they will know who is worse in place and weaker in troops" (19:75), in contrast with "better in station and finer in assembly," because their station is their place and their dwelling?

Al-nadiyy: the assembly that gathers the notables of their people, their helpers and their supporters. Al-jund: they are the helpers and the supporters.

And (as for) "wa-yazidu" (and He increases): it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the place (mawdi') of "fa-l-yamdud" (let him extend), since it occupies the position of a predicate (khabar). Its implied sense: "whoever is in error, the Most Merciful will extend (his term) for him, or He will extend it for him." "Wa-yazidu" means: He increases the error of the one who strays, by abandoning him, and He increases the guided in guidance, by granting them success.

"Wa-l-baqiyatu al-salihatu" (and the enduring good deeds): these are all the deeds of the Hereafter. It has been said: the prayers. It has been said: "Subhan Allah, wa-l-hamdu li-Allah, wa-la ilaha illa Allah, wa-Allahu akbar." That is, they are "khayrun thawaban" (better in reward) than the boasting of the disbelievers, "wa-khayrun maraddan" (and better in return), i.e., in place of return and in outcome, or in benefit, from the saying: "laysa li-hadha al-amri marudd" (there is no turning back from this matter):

"Wa-hal yarudda bukay zandan" [[The explanation of this line of evidence has passed in the second part, page 525; refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector)]]

If you ask: how is it said "khayrun thawaban" as though their boasting had a reward, so that the reward of the good deeds is made better than it? I answer: it is as if it were said: their reward is the Fire, in the manner of his saying: "... fa-a'tibu bi-l-sayyalam" [[The explanation of this line of evidence has passed in the first part, page 105; refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector)]]

And his saying:

"Shaj'a'a jarratha al-dhumayli talukuhu ... asalan idha rah al-matiyyu ghurathan" [[Al-shaj'a': quickness in the movement of the legs. Al-shaj'a'a: swift in its pace. Al-jirrah (with kasra): what a camel regurgitates from its stomach and chews. Al-dhumayl: a kind of pace. Al-luk: chewing. Al-asal: plural of asil, which is from afternoon to sunset. Al-rawah: from noon to it. Al-ghurath: the hungry. He describes his she-camel by swiftness of pace, and he likens the pace of it to its cud, combining swiftness of motion, the camel's ease and its relish for each. And he made her bring it forth little by little, like the cud, for emphasis. In it is an indication of her stomach being empty of fodder when she departs, i.e., when others cannot find strength to walk, so "al-ghurath" is a metaphor. It is also permissible that the meaning is that she is swift in pace even if she is hungry like other mounts, so "al-ghurath" is literal.]]

And his saying:

"Tahiyyatun baynahum darbun waji'" [[The explanation of this line of evidence has passed in the first part, page 60; refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector)]]

Then he built upon it "khayrun thawaban." In it is a form of mockery (tahakkum), which is more enraging to the one threatened than it would be to say to him: "your reward is the Fire." If you ask: what is the basis of the comparative in "khayr," as though their boasting had a share in it? I answer: this is from the concise speech of their people; they say: "al-sayfu ahharu min al-shitai" (summer is hotter than winter), i.e., it is more intense than winter in its cold.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verses 77–80:

Since seeing and observing things is a path to comprehending them with knowledge and to the soundness of reports about them, they used *a-ra'ayta* ("have you seen?") in the sense of *akhbir* ("tell me"). The *fa'* (then) came to convey its meaning, which is sequence (ta'aqqub), as if he had said: "Tell me also the story of this disbeliever, and mention his account right after the account of those others." ﴿Has he looked into the unseen...﴾ comes from their saying:

*Atla'a al-jabal*: when he climbed to its summit and ascended the pass (*al-thaniyya*). [[His words "wa-tala'a al-thaniyya" (and ascended the pass): in al-Sihah, "talaʿtu al-jabal" (with kasra): I climbed it. (ʿ)]] Jarir said:

*Laqitu mutta'a al-jibali waʿūran*
(I met the steep ascents of the mountains, rugged ones.)

[[The line of Jarir: "Inni idha Mudar ʿalayya tahaddathat... laqitu mutta'a al-jibali waʿūran." *Mudar* is the name of a tribe, declined for the sake of metre. *Mutta'* (with a doubled ṭā') is a noun of place in the form of the passive participle, from *ittala'a* (intensive), originally *ittatala'a*, with the ta' of the reflexive form changed to ṭā' and the preceding letter assimilated into it. It is in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarfiyya). *Wu'ūr* is the plural of *wa'r*, meaning difficult. It is the object of *laqītu*, or the object is *muṭṭala'*. *Wa'ūran* is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), especially on the reading with the vowel of the *waw* opened, as an intensive form. The meaning: if they speak against Mudar something I do not approve, or talk about their dead, I find in the ascents of the mountains difficult things, and I am unable to flee. Or the meaning is that he plunges into difficulties without caring and flees from them. On the circumstantial reading: "I met the ascents of the mountains while they were difficult places." The *mutta'* is plural because it is attached to a plural noun. On the reading with the *waw* opened, the meaning is clear.]]

They also say: *marra muṭṭali'an li-dhalika al-amr*, meaning: he was high over that matter, master of it. The choice of this word is significant. [[Another poet says]]:

Has he reached such greatness of station that he has climbed to the knowledge of the unseen, which belongs exclusively to the One, the Subduer? The meaning is that what he claims to be given and swears he will receive can only be reached by one of two ways: either knowledge of the unseen, or a covenant from the Lord of the unseen. So by which of these did he reach that?

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *wuldan* (with a ḍammah on the wāw and the lām), which is the plural of *walad*, like *asad* in *usud*. Or it means the same as *walad*, like *al-ʿarab* in *al-ʿarab*. From Yahya ibn Ya'mur: *waladan* (with a kasra on the lām). It was said about *ʿahd* (covenant): the statement of testimony (kalimat al-shahada). From Qatada: "Has he done a righteous deed beforehand, so that he hopes by it for what he says?" From al-Kalbi: "Has God made a covenant with him that He will give him that?"

From al-Hasan, may God have mercy on him: it was revealed about al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. The well-known view is that it was revealed about al-As ibn Wa'il. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: "I had a debt owed to him, and I asked him for it. He said: 'No, by God, not until you disbelieve in Muhammad.' I said: 'No, by God, I will not disbelieve in Muhammad, alive or dead, nor even when you are resurrected.' He said: 'When I die and am resurrected, will I come back?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'When I am resurrected I will come to you, and I will have wealth and children, and then I will pay you.'" [[Agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), from the chain of Masruq from Khabbab, more complete than this.]] It was also said: Khabbab made him a piece of jewellery and asked for his wage, and he said: "You claim that you will be resurrected, and that in Paradise there is gold, silver and silk. I will pay you then, for I will be given wealth and children at that time."

*Kalla* (No!) is a rebuke and a warning about the error. That is: he is mistaken in what he imagines for himself and wishes for; let him desist from it.

If you ask: why did He say ﴿We will record﴾ with the *sin* of future deferment, when recording is as He said: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is an observer ready﴾? I say: there are two possibilities. First: "We will make him know and we will show him that We have recorded his words," in the manner of the saying of the poet:

*Idha ma intasabna lam talidani lu'aymatun*
*Ramatni ʿan qawsi al-ʿaduwwi wa-ba'idat*
*ʿUbayda zada Allahu ma baynana buʿdan*

(When we trace our lineage, you did not give birth to me as a base woman. / She shot me from the bow of the enemy, and made the distance wide. / May God increase what is between us in distance, O Ubayda.)

These lines are by Za'id ibn Sa'sa'a al-Naq'asi. He had a wife named Ubayda who was disloyal to him, and her mother was a slave-woman. He alluded to this, saying: "She shot me with a shameful matter, as if it were an arrow flying from the enemy's bow, or she put me far from her, as far as the arrow is from the bow" (that is, she was the cause of it and exaggerated in the distance of the shot). "May God increase" is a prayer. Then he said: "When we make our lineage known, it will become clear that I was not born of a base woman, unlike you, and you will find no escape or refuge from acknowledging that matter." It is also permissible that the meaning is: you must acknowledge your base mother, and the reference of the pronoun is known from the mention of the contrast, which is his mother. This is more precise in rebuke. It is also related as *bihi* (by it), meaning: by that lineage. The shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second contains a kind of reproach and denunciation, as if he first wondered at her condition, then turned to rebuke her for the baseness of her mother and that she was a slave. [[The meaning: it becomes clear and known by the claim of lineage that I am not the son of a base woman.]] The second possibility: the one who threatens says to the wrongdoer, "I will surely take revenge on you," meaning that he does not fail in retribution even if time is prolonged and delayed. So here the verb is used in the sense of threat. ﴿And We will extend for him of the punishment an extension﴾, that is: We will lengthen for him from the punishment what he deserves, and punish him with the kind of punishment with which the mocking disbelievers are punished. Or: We will increase him in punishment and multiply his respite (*madad*). It is said: *madda* and *amadda* have the same meaning. The reading of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib supports this: *wa-namudda lahu* with a ḍammah. He emphasized it with the verbal noun (maṣdar), which comes from the intensity of God's anger, from which we seek refuge in Him from what would make us deserve His wrath.

﴿And We will inherit from him what he says﴾: that is, We will withdraw from him what he claims he will attain in the Hereafter, and give it to one who deserves it. The meaning is: "his claim." What he says is wealth and children. A man says: "I possess such-and-such," and you say to him: "I have more than what you say." It is possible that he desired and hoped that God would give him wealth and children in this world, and his greed (*ashʿabiyya*) [[His words "ashʿabiyya": in al-Sihah, "Ashʿab" is the name of a man who was very greedy. In the proverb: "More greedy than Ashʿab." From it: "akhadhat al-ashʿabiyya," meaning: the trait of Ashʿab, which is greed. (ʿ)]] carried him to swear an oath concerning that in His words ﴿I will surely be given﴾, because it is the answer to a hidden oath. And whoever swears by God, God will disprove him. So God, mighty and majestic, says: "Suppose We gave him what he desired: either We inherit it from him in the end, and he will come to Us alone tomorrow, without wealth or children, as in His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿And you have come to Us alone...﴾ — the verse. So his wish and his oath will not benefit him."

It is also possible that he says this only while he is alive. When We take his soul, We will prevent him from saying it, and he will come to Us rejecting it, separated from it, not saying it. Or We will not forget this saying of his, nor nullify it, but We will record it in his record, so that We may strike his face with it at the place of standing, and reproach him with it. ﴿And he will come to Us﴾ in his poverty and humiliation ﴿alone﴾, without wealth or children. We did not grant him his request nor give him what he hoped for, so both calamities gather upon him: the consequence of his words and their burden, and the loss of what he coveted.

*Fardan* (alone) in the first interpretation is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) with a future sense, like ﴿enter it to abide therein﴾, because he and others are equal in coming alone at the time of arrival, and then they differ after that.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verse 84:

"Ajjaltu 'alayhi bi-kadhā" (I hastened him toward such-and-such) means: when you ask him to hasten it for you. That is: do not hasten against them (the disbelievers) that they be destroyed and annihilated, so that you and the Muslims may be relieved of their evils and the earth be purified by cutting off their last traces. There remains between you and what you seek of their destruction only a limited number of days and counted breaths, as if, in its swiftness, it were the hour that is counted when one counts it. A similar statement is His Exalted saying: ﴿And do not be hasty for them. It is as if, on the day they see what they are promised, they had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [46:35]. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that when he recited it, he would weep and say: "The last of the count is the departure of your soul; the last of the count is the separation from your family; the last of the count is the entry into your grave." And it is related from Ibn al-Sammak that he was in the presence of al-Ma'mun when he recited it, and he said: "If breaths are counted and there is no replenishment for them, how quickly they are exhausted."

Its accusative (naṣb) is governed by an implied verb: "the day when We gather (naḥshuru) and drive (nasūqu)": We shall deal with both groups in a manner that no description can encompass. Or: "Remember the day when We gather." It is also permissible for it to be governed by "they will not possess" (lā yamlikūna).

The righteous (al-muttaqūn) are mentioned with the wording of honour (al-tabjīl), namely that they are gathered to their Lord, who has overwhelmed them with His mercy and singled them out for His good pleasure and generosity, just as delegations (wufūd) come to kings, awaiting honour in their presence.

It is related from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "They will not be gathered on their feet, by Allah, but on camels whose saddle-frames are gold, and on swift mounts whose saddles are rubies." [Narrated by Ibn Abī Shaybah and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Aḥmad in the Zawāʾid of the Musnad, and by al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim from the narration of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Isḥāq ibn al-Nuʿmān ibn Saʿd ibn ʿAlī, similarly; and Ibn Abī Dāwūd in the Kitāb al-Baʿth narrated it through this route as a marfūʿ (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) report. Ibn ʿAdī also related it as a marfūʿ hadith from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both.]

Al-Zamakhshari, *al-Kashshaf*, on Surah 19, verse 86:

The disbelievers are described as being driven to the Fire with humiliation and contempt, like thirsty livestock driven to water. *Al-Warud* (the thirsty, those brought to water) means the thirsty, because one who comes to water comes only out of thirst. The real meaning of *al-wird* is going to water. The poet said:

*Ridi, ridi, the coming to water of a deaf sand-grouse,*
*Like a kadriyya, delighted by the coolness of the water.*

The poet is addressing his she-camel. *Ridi* is an imperative from *al-wurud*, and its repetition is for emphasis. *Al-wird* is also a verbal noun from it, or a name for the water that is come to. The meaning is: go to the water as a deaf sand-grouse comes to water, one that does not hear the hunter's sound and so does not flee from the water. *Al-kadr* (with a *damma*) is a kind of sand-grouse with a dusty colour. *Kadriyya* is its relative form, a nisba from the singular to the collective, and this *ya* is the one that distinguishes the singular from the noun of kind, as in *rum* and *rumi*. In it there is an implicit comparison of the she-camel to the sand-grouse in lightness and speed. *Samma* and *al-ma* are pronounced with a short vowel. If the rhyme is read with a long vowel and sukun, then the metre is from the *mashtur* form of *al-munsarih*, *al-mawquf* (a truncated, pausal form of the *munsarih* metre), and its place is the letter *alif*.

Hence those who come to the water are called *al-waridun* (those who come to water). Al-Hasan recited: "The righteous will be gathered" and "the criminals will be driven."

The waw in *lā yamlikūna* could be a pronoun (ḍamīr) [Maḥmūd said: "It is possible that the waw in *lā yamlikūna* is a pronoun..." etc.]. Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: In this view there is some strain (taʿassuf), because when it is made a marker (ʿalāma) for a plural, and its meaning has been uncovered and made clear that it refers to a plural group, then the pronoun of *ittakhadha* is referred back to its wording in the singular. That involves returning to its wording after returning to its meaning, in a way that contradicts it, and this is considered objectionable by them, because it is vagueness after clarity, and that is an inversion in the method of eloquence (balāgha). The clear path of eloquence is clarity after vagueness. The waw, according to its grammatical analysis (iʿrāb), even if it does not refer back to *man*, nevertheless reveals its meaning just as a referring pronoun does. So pay attention to this necklace, for it is more current than criticism:

"And on the neck of the beautiful woman the necklace looks good."

So it refers to the servants (ʿibād), and the mention of the pious (*al-muttaqūn*) and the guilty (*al-mujrimūn*) indicates this, because they are in this division. It is also permissible that it be a marker of the plural, like the one in *"akalūnī al-barāghīth"* (the fleas ate me), and the agent (fāʿil) is *man ittakhadha*, because it has the meaning of the plural. The position (maḥall) of *man ittakhadha* is nominative (rafʿ) as a substitute (badal), or as an agent. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative on the assumption of an omitted noun (muḍāf), meaning: *illā shafāʿata man ittakhadha* (except the intercession of one who took). The intended meaning is: they do not possess the ability to intercede for them. Taking a covenant (ʿahd) means seeking support through faith and action. It is related from Ibn Masʿūd that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his companions one day: "Is one of you unable to take a covenant with God every morning and evening?" They said: "And how is that?" He said: "Let him say every morning and evening: O God, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the visible, I make a covenant with You that I bear witness that there is no god but You alone, without partner, and that Muḥammad is Your servant and Messenger, and that if You leave me to myself You bring me near to evil and distance me from good, and that I trust only in Your mercy; so grant me with You a covenant that You will fulfil for me on the Day of Resurrection, for You do not break the promise." When he says that, it is sealed with a seal and placed beneath the Throne. When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller calls out: "Where are those who have a covenant with the All-Merciful?" and they enter Paradise. [Al-Thaʿlabī reported it: Abū Wāʾil narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd—and he mentioned it in full. Ibn Mardawayh also related in his *Tafsīr al-Aḥzāb*, through ʿAwf ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from a man of the Banū Sulaym, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd (may God be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The covenant is that you say: O God, Originator of the heavens and the earth..." — the hadith is shorter than what was mentioned. Al-Ḥākim related it by another route, from ʿAwn, from Ibn Māja, from al-Aswad, from Ibn Masʿūd, that he recited this verse: "Except one who has taken a covenant with the All-Merciful" and said: God the Exalted says, on the Day of Resurrection: "Whoever has a covenant with Me, let him stand." Then we said: "Teach us, O Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān." He said: "Recite: O God, Originator of the heavens and the earth..." — mentioned in brief. And on this subject there is also a report from Abū Bakr (may God be pleased with him), which al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī recorded in *al-Nawādir*, in the seventy-sixth section after the hundredth.] It is also said: it is the statement of the testimony (kalimat al-shahāda). Or it may be from "the ruler made a covenant to so-and-so with such-and-such" when he commanded him with it, meaning: no one intercedes except the one commanded to intercede and permitted to do so. This is supported by passages in the revelation: ﴿And how many an angel in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing except after God permits whom He wills and approves.﴾ And ﴿Intercession with Him avails nothing except for one whom He has permitted.﴾ And ﴿On that Day intercession will not avail except for one whom the All-Merciful has permitted and whose word He approves.﴾

The Qira'at (readings) of **idd** are both with a kasra and with a fatha. Ibn Khalawayh said: *al-idd* and *al-add* mean "wonder," and it is also said they mean "something great and objectionable." *Al-iddah* means "severity." *Adnā al-amr* and *ādnā* mean: it burdened me and was great upon me. The reading of al-Kisa'i and Nafi' is with a ya'. ﴿Takādu (يَتَفَطَّرْنَ)﴾ is recited with ya'. The reading of "yanfaṭirna" is recorded. *Al-infiṭār* comes from *faṭarahu*, when he split it. *Al-tafaṭṭur* comes from *faṭṭarahu*, when he split it, with the verb repeated in it. Ibn Mas'ud read *yanṣadi'na*, meaning they are split apart. It means "they are crushed with a crushing," or "crushed," or it is an object of purpose, meaning: because they are crushed.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the splitting of the heavens, the cleaving of the earth, and the falling down of the mountains? And from where does this word affect inanimate things? I say: there are two aspects to this. The first is that Allah, glory be to Him, says: "I was about to do this to the heavens and the earth." [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: I was about to crush the heavens and split the earth... etc." Ahmad says: another meaning appears to me beyond these, and Allah knows best. Allah the Exalted, in order to indicate His existence described by the perfect attributes that are necessary for Him, made them glorify Him. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him, and there is nothing except that it glorifies His praise﴾ [17:44]. Among what the heavens, the earth and the mountains indicate, indeed every atom of them, is that Allah the Exalted is exalted above having a child ascribed to Him. "And in everything there is a sign of Him, indicating that He is One." So the one who believes that Allah has a child has nullified the indication of these existing things to the purification and sanctification of Allah. Therefore the destruction of their forms by crushing, splitting and cleaving is used metaphorically to nullify the spirit of indication for which they were created. Glory be to the One who divided His servants, so He made some servants enjoy and glorify with the glorification of Dawud; the heavens nearly crumble at his saying, from one who is far from the door of success, rejected and turned away.]] And the mountains, when this word is uttered, are in anger from Me against the one who uttered it, were it not for My forbearance and dignity, and that I do not hasten punishment, as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they ceased, none could hold them after Him. Indeed He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving﴾ [35:41].

The second aspect: that this is an exaggeration of the word and an amplification of its enormity, and a depiction of its effect on religion and its demolition of its pillars and foundations. The example of that effect in tangible things is that it strikes these great bodies, which are the pillars of the world, so that they are split, cleaved and fall down.

In His saying ﴿Certainly you have brought something hideous﴾ [19:89], and what is in it of address after the third person, which is called *al-iltifat* (the shift in grammatical person, from absence to address) in the science of rhetoric, is an added rebuke against them for their audacity against Allah, and for exposing themselves to His wrath, and an alert to the magnitude of what they said.

For ﴿أَنْ دَعَوْا﴾ [that they ascribed] there are three possibilities. It may be in the genitive as a substitute for the pronoun in *minhu* (from it), as in the poet's words:

"In a state where, if Hatim were among the people, with his generosity he would be stingy with water."

[[The explanation of this evidence was given in the first volume, page 438; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

Or it may be in the accusative, by the omission of the preposition *al-lam* and the verb's reaching its object, meaning: because they ascribed, so the falling down was caused by the crushing, and the crushing by the ascribing of a child to the Most Merciful. Or it may be in the nominative, as the subject of *hadha* (this), meaning: its crushing is the ascribing of a child to the Most Merciful.

In the specification of *al-Rahman* and its repetition several times, there is the benefit that He alone is the Most Merciful, and no one else deserves this name, because the roots of blessings and their branches come from Him: He created the worlds and created for them everything they have. As one of them said: "Let His covering be removed from your sight, for you and all that you possess are His gift." So whoever ascribes a child to Him has made him like one of His creatures, and by that has removed him from deserving the name *al-Rahman*.

*Min da'a* here means "named," which is transitive to two objects, and it was limited to one of them, which is the second, seeking generality and comprehensiveness over everything for which He is named with a child. Or *min da'a* means "attributed," whose intransitive form is what appears in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever claims descent from other than his masters..." [[I have not seen it with the wording "whoever claims"; rather it is in Muslim with the wording "inntama", narrated from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib, raised: "Whoever claims descent from other than his father or attaches himself to other than his masters..." the hadith.]] And the poet's words:

"We, the sons of Nahshal, do not claim to be of a father other than ourselves, nor does he buy us with his sons.
It suffices him, if we die, that he is pleased with us, and when the fathers are mentioned, he suffices us."

These are by Bashama ibn Hazn al-Nahshali. It is said: "So-and-so claimed among the Banu Hashim, and for them, and to them," meaning he attributed himself to them, and "he claimed from them" when he attributed himself to others. He turned from them, saying: we do not claim descent from a father other than Nahshal. "The sons of Nahshal" is in the accusative by specification, which indicates praise. "Nor does he buy us" means he does not sell us and exchange us for the sons of others. Then he said: it suffices him from us that he is pleased with us if we die and join him, since we have made for him and for us the beautiful praise of our bravery and good qualities. "In" here means "when," because death is undoubted. It is narrated as "an yasubba" with a ba', and perhaps its meaning is: there is no reproach for him except our death in battle, meaning: if that were a reproach, and it is not so. It is possible that his expression "sufficiency" indicates that he is independent of praise from the side of his sons when boasting, and when counting the glories of the fathers, we do not need anyone else, so we are attributed to him in order to be honored by his honor.

That is, we do not attribute ourselves to him.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 19, verses 93–95:**

*Man* is descriptive (*mawsufa*, a relative-type indefinite) because it occurs after every indefinite noun, and its occurrence after *rubba* in his saying:

*Rubba man anḍajtu ghayẓan ṣadrahu* [[Rubba man anḍajtu ghayẓan qalbahu ... qad tamanna lī mawtan lam yuṭa'

wa-yarānī ka-l-shajā fī ḥalqihi ... 'usran makhrajuhu mā yantazi'

lam yaḍurrunī ghayra an yaḥsudanī ... fa-huwa yazqū mithla mā yazqū al-ḍū'

wa-yuḥyīnī idhā lāqaytuhu ... wa-idhā yakhlū lahu laḥmī ra'ta'

These lines are by Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil al-Yashkuri. It is necessarily the case that *man* is an indefinite descriptive noun, because *rubba* only governs an indefinite noun. The ripening (*nuḍj*) of meat and grapes and the like means that they became ripe (*naḍīj* and *nāḍij*): they reached maturity, attained their proper time, and were fully cooked. That is, "many a person whose heart was cooked by the heat of his rage at me, and who did not obey (i.e., it cannot be endured because of its cause)." *Al-shajā* is what lodges in the throat, such as a bone or the like. *'Usran* etc.: it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from him. *Makhrajuhu*, i.e., its exit, is raised by the descriptive adjective. "He did not harm me in any way except through envy." *Ḍayr* is from *ḍāra yaḍīru ḍayran*, when he harms him. "So he cries out (*yazqū*), i.e., he screams like the screaming of the *al-ḍū'*, which is the male of the day (a bird)." The comparison of the impugned honour to eaten meat is very common, by way of the explicit metaphor (*taṣrīḥiyya*). Then the poet compared him to a fertile pasture in which beasts graze (*tarta'*). Or he likened the backbiter to a beast in pasture, by way of the implicit metaphor (*makniyya*), and *al-ra'ta'* is an imaginative representation (*takhyīl*). It is also possible that the poet borrowed eating, which suits meat, and then attacking, which suits honour, by way of explicit metaphor. That is: "when he is alone with me, he backbites as he wishes."

And Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Haywa read ﴿Ātī al-Raḥmān﴾ (*Ātī al-Raḥmāni*), in accordance with its original form before the *idāfa* (annexation). *Al-iḥṣā'* is enumeration and precise control, meaning: He has confined them by His knowledge and surrounded them. ﴿He has enumerated them and counted them with exact counting﴾.

Those who believed that the angels, Jesus and 'Uzayr were the children of God were between two kinds of disbelief. One was the claim that the Most Merciful could be a father. The second was associating with God those whom they claimed to be His children in worship, just as people serve the sons of kings in the way they serve their fathers. So God demolished the first disbelief in the verses preceding this, then followed it with the demolition of the other disbelief.

The meaning is: there is no one whom they worship in the heavens and the earth, of the angels or of mankind, except that he comes to the Most Merciful, i.e., he takes refuge in Him and seeks shelter in His lordship as a servant who is submissive, obedient, humble, fearful and hopeful, as servants do and as it is obligatory upon them to do. He does not claim for himself what these misguided people claim for him. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek the means of access to their Lord, [each of them] which is nearest, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment﴾.

All of them are subject to His dominion, overpowered by His power, and He is watchful over them, encompassing them, and in charge of their affairs, their details, their states and their numbers. Nothing of their circumstances escapes Him. Each one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone, with none of these polytheists with him, and they will be free of them.

Jinah ibn Habish recited *wuddan* with a kasra (*widdan*). The meaning is: Allah will bring about love (*mawaddah*) in their hearts for them, planting it for them there without any effort on their part to win affection and without any pursuit of the causes that produce love, through which people gain the affection of hearts, such as kinship, friendship, doing good to others, or other things. The *sin* (in *sa-yaj'alu*, "He will bring about") may be taken in one of two ways. It may refer to the fact that the sura is Meccan, when the believers were despised among the disbelievers, so Allah promised them this once Islam had spread. Or it may refer to the Day of Resurrection, when He will make them beloved to His creation by means of the good deeds that appear for them and the records of their deeds that are published.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: O Jibril, I love so-and-so, so love him.
